## 2.2 Core DNS Service Features

### 2.2.1 DNS Forwarding and Caching (F-001)

#### 2.2.1.1 Feature Metadata

| Attribute | Value |
|-----------|-------|
| **Feature ID** | F-001 |
| **Feature Name** | DNS Forwarding and Caching |
| **Category** | Core DNS Services |
| **Priority** | Critical |

| Attribute | Value |
|-----------|-------|
| **Status** | Completed |
| **Complexity** | Medium |
| **Source Files** | `src/forward.c`, `src/cache.c`, `src/rfc1035.c` |

#### 2.2.1.2 Description

**Overview**

DNS Forwarding and Caching provides lightweight DNS resolution services for small networks by accepting DNS queries from downstream clients, consulting a local cache, and forwarding cache misses to configured upstream recursive DNS servers. The system implements efficient caching with configurable capacity, TTL management, and integration with local hostname sources.

**Business Value**

- Reduces upstream bandwidth consumption by caching frequently accessed DNS records locally
- Improves DNS query response latency through sub-millisecond cache hit responses
- Eliminates the need for complex recursive DNS server deployment in small network environments
- Provides unified DNS namespace integrating upstream DNS, local `/etc/hosts` entries, and DHCP lease hostnames

**User Benefits**

- Network administrators benefit from zero-configuration DNS deployment with automatic upstream server discovery from `/etc/resolv.conf`
- End users experience faster web browsing and application performance through reduced DNS resolution latency
- Small networks gain enterprise-class DNS caching without resource overhead of full recursive resolvers

**Technical Context**

The DNS forwarding engine implements a stateful query forwarding mechanism that tracks outstanding queries, manages UDP and TCP transport protocols, implements proper timeout and retry logic, and handles DNS wire format parsing per RFC 1035. The cache uses a least-recently-used (LRU) eviction policy with configurable sizing (default 150 entries, defined by `CACHESIZ` in `src/config.h` line 38).

#### 2.2.1.3 Dependencies

| Dependency Type | Description |
|----------------|-------------|
| **Prerequisite Features** | None (core feature) |
| **System Dependencies** | `/etc/resolv.conf` for upstream DNS servers, `/etc/hosts` for local hostname resolution |

| Dependency Type | Description |
|----------------|-------------|
| **External Dependencies** | Standard C library (libc), POSIX sockets API |
| **Integration Requirements** | Optional: inotify for dynamic configuration reload (Linux) |

#### 2.2.1.4 Functional Requirements

| Requirement ID | Description | Priority |
|---------------|-------------|----------|
| F-001-RQ-001 | Accept DNS queries on UDP port 53 from configured network interfaces | Must-Have |
| F-001-RQ-002 | Accept DNS queries on TCP port 53 for large responses and zone transfers | Must-Have |

| Requirement ID | Description | Priority |
|---------------|-------------|----------|
| F-001-RQ-003 | Implement local DNS cache with LRU eviction policy | Must-Have |
| F-001-RQ-004 | Cache A, AAAA, CNAME, PTR, DNSKEY, and DS record types | Must-Have |

| Requirement ID | Description | Complexity |
|---------------|-------------|------------|
| F-001-RQ-005 | Forward cache miss queries to upstream DNS servers | Low |
| F-001-RQ-006 | Implement query timeout mechanism (default 10 seconds) | Low |

| Requirement ID | Description | Complexity |
|---------------|-------------|------------|
| F-001-RQ-007 | Integrate `/etc/hosts` file entries into DNS resolution | Low |
| F-001-RQ-008 | Integrate DHCP lease hostnames into DNS namespace | Medium |

**Detailed Requirements Table**

| Requirement ID | Acceptance Criteria | Performance Criteria |
|---------------|---------------------|---------------------|
| F-001-RQ-001 | UDP socket successfully bound to port 53; queries received and parsed correctly | Response latency <1ms for cached entries |
| F-001-RQ-002 | TCP socket successfully bound to port 53; connection handling for large queries | Max 100 queries per TCP connection (TCP_MAX_QUERIES) |
| F-001-RQ-003 | Cache stores minimum 150 entries (default); LRU eviction verified under load | Cache lookup latency <0.1ms |
| F-001-RQ-004 | Each record type cached correctly with TTL expiration; negative caching for NXDOMAIN | Memory consumption ~100-200 bytes per record |

| Requirement ID | Input Parameters | Output/Response |
|---------------|------------------|----------------|
| F-001-RQ-005 | DNS query packet (UDP/TCP), configured upstream servers | DNS response packet from upstream or timeout error |
| F-001-RQ-006 | Query timeout configuration (default 10s, TIMEOUT in config.h:30) | Query failure response after timeout expiration |
| F-001-RQ-007 | `/etc/hosts` file contents, DNS query for hostname | DNS A/AAAA record response from hosts file |
| F-001-RQ-008 | DHCP lease database with hostnames, DNS query | DNS A/AAAA record response for DHCP client hostname |

**Validation Rules**

| Requirement ID | Business Rules | Data Validation |
|---------------|----------------|----------------|
| F-001-RQ-001 | Only respond to queries from configured allowed interfaces | DNS packet format validation per RFC 1035 |
| F-001-RQ-003 | Cache size configurable via `--cache-size` option; 0 disables caching | Cache entry TTL must be non-negative integer |
| F-001-RQ-005 | Domain-specific upstream routing per configuration | Upstream server must be valid IP address |
| F-001-RQ-006 | Timeout applies to upstream queries only, not cached responses | Timeout value must be positive integer |

| Requirement ID | Security Requirements | Compliance Requirements |
|---------------|---------------------|------------------------|
| F-001-RQ-001 | Source port randomization for outbound queries | RFC 1035 (DNS protocol) |
| F-001-RQ-002 | TCP connection limits prevent DoS (MAX_PROCS=20) | RFC 1035 (DNS over TCP) |
| F-001-RQ-008 | DHCP hostnames validated against DNS naming rules | RFC 1123 (hostname requirements) |

### 2.2.2 DNSSEC Validation (F-002)

#### 2.2.2.1 Feature Metadata

| Attribute | Value |
|-----------|-------|
| **Feature ID** | F-002 |
| **Feature Name** | DNSSEC Validation |
| **Category** | Core DNS Services |
| **Priority** | Medium |

| Attribute | Value |
|-----------|-------|
| **Status** | Completed |
| **Complexity** | High |
| **Source Files** | `src/dnssec.c`, `src/crypto.c` |

#### 2.2.2.2 Description

**Overview**

DNSSEC Validation provides cryptographic validation of DNS responses to protect against DNS cache poisoning, man-in-the-middle attacks, and DNS spoofing. The system verifies RRSIG signatures, validates DNSKEY and DS records, processes NSEC/NSEC3 denial-of-existence proofs, and maintains trust anchors for the DNS root zone.

**Business Value**

- Protects users from DNS-based attacks including cache poisoning and domain hijacking
- Ensures DNS response integrity and authenticity through cryptographic validation
- Meets security compliance requirements for networks requiring validated DNS resolution
- Provides foundation for secure DNS infrastructure without requiring separate DNSSEC validator deployment

**User Benefits**

- Network administrators gain enterprise-grade DNS security in resource-constrained environments
- End users are protected from malicious DNS responses without additional client configuration
- Organizations can enforce DNSSEC validation policy through single configuration point

**Technical Context**

DNSSEC validation implements RFC 4033, 4034, and 4035 specifications using the Nettle cryptography library for signature verification operations. The implementation enforces configurable limits to prevent denial-of-service attacks: maximum 40 queries per validation (DNSSEC_LIMIT_WORK), maximum 20 signature failures (DNSSEC_LIMIT_SIG_FAIL), maximum 200 crypto operations (DNSSEC_LIMIT_CRYPTO), and maximum 150 NSEC3 iterations (DNSSEC_LIMIT_NSEC3_ITERS) as defined in `src/config.h` lines 25-29.

#### 2.2.2.3 Dependencies

| Dependency Type | Description |
|----------------|-------------|
| **Prerequisite Features** | F-001 (DNS Forwarding and Caching) |
| **System Dependencies** | Trust anchor configuration file: `trust-anchors.conf` (current as of July 2024) |

| Dependency Type | Description |
|----------------|-------------|
| **External Dependencies** | Nettle cryptography library (libnettle, libhogweed); optional: libgmp for multi-precision arithmetic |
| **Integration Requirements** | Compile-time flag: HAVE_DNSSEC; upstream DNS servers must support DNSSEC |

#### 2.2.2.4 Functional Requirements

| Requirement ID | Description | Priority |
|---------------|-------------|----------|
| F-002-RQ-001 | Verify RRSIG signatures for DNSSEC-signed responses | Must-Have |
| F-002-RQ-002 | Validate DNSKEY records against DS records in parent zone | Must-Have |

| Requirement ID | Description | Priority |
|---------------|-------------|----------|
| F-002-RQ-003 | Process NSEC records for authenticated denial of existence | Must-Have |
| F-002-RQ-004 | Process NSEC3 records with iteration limit enforcement | Must-Have |

| Requirement ID | Description | Complexity |
|---------------|-------------|------------|
| F-002-RQ-005 | Maintain trust anchor chain from root zone to target domain | High |
| F-002-RQ-006 | Return SERVFAIL for failed DNSSEC validation (bogus responses) | Medium |

| Requirement ID | Description | Complexity |
|---------------|-------------|------------|
| F-002-RQ-007 | Implement DNSSEC validation resource limits to prevent DoS | Medium |
| F-002-RQ-008 | Support RFC 8914 extended DNS errors for detailed failure reporting | Low |

**Detailed Requirements Table**

| Requirement ID | Acceptance Criteria | Performance Criteria |
|---------------|---------------------|---------------------|
| F-002-RQ-001 | RRSIG signature verification succeeds for valid signatures; fails for invalid | Crypto operations limited to 200 per query |
| F-002-RQ-002 | DNSKEY validation traverses chain to trust anchor successfully | Maximum 40 queries per validation chain |
| F-002-RQ-003 | NSEC denial-of-existence proofs accepted for non-existent names | Processing latency <50ms per NSEC |
| F-002-RQ-004 | NSEC3 iteration count validated against limit (max 150 iterations) | NSEC3 processing rejected if iterations exceed limit |

| Requirement ID | Input Parameters | Output/Response |
|---------------|------------------|----------------|
| F-002-RQ-005 | Trust anchors from `trust-anchors.conf`, DNSKEY/DS records from DNS | Validated trust chain or validation failure |
| F-002-RQ-006 | Failed DNSSEC validation result | SERVFAIL response code to client |
| F-002-RQ-007 | DNSSEC query processing limits from config.h | Query aborted if limits exceeded |
| F-002-RQ-008 | Validation failure reason | Extended DNS error code in response (when supported) |

**Validation Rules**

| Requirement ID | Business Rules | Data Validation |
|---------------|----------------|----------------|
| F-002-RQ-001 | RRSIG inception and expiration times must be current | Signature algorithm must be supported |
| F-002-RQ-002 | DS record hash algorithm must match DNSKEY | DNSKEY flags must indicate zone-signing key |
| F-002-RQ-004 | NSEC3 iterations must not exceed DNSSEC_LIMIT_NSEC3_ITERS (150) | NSEC3 hash algorithm must be supported |
| F-002-RQ-007 | Signature failures limited to 20 per validation | Crypto operations limited to 200 per query |

| Requirement ID | Security Requirements | Compliance Requirements |
|---------------|---------------------|------------------------|
| F-002-RQ-001 | Cryptographic signature verification using Nettle library | RFC 4034 (DNSSEC resource records) |
| F-002-RQ-005 | Trust anchor validation against root zone KSK | RFC 4035 (DNSSEC protocol) |
| F-002-RQ-006 | Failed validation must not return potentially malicious data | RFC 4033 (DNSSEC security considerations) |
| F-002-RQ-008 | Extended error codes per RFC 8914 | RFC 8914 (extended DNS errors) |

### 2.2.3 Authoritative DNS Mode (F-008)

#### 2.2.3.1 Feature Metadata

| Attribute | Value |
|-----------|-------|
| **Feature ID** | F-008 |
| **Feature Name** | Authoritative DNS Mode |
| **Category** | Core DNS Services |
| **Priority** | Medium |

| Attribute | Value |
|-----------|-------|
| **Status** | Completed |
| **Complexity** | Medium |
| **Source Files** | `src/auth.c` |

#### 2.2.3.2 Description

**Overview**

Authoritative DNS Mode enables dnsmasq to serve as a primary nameserver for designated local zones, responding authoritatively to queries within those zones and supporting zone transfers (AXFR) to secondary nameservers. This capability complements the forwarding mode by allowing dnsmasq to host small DNS zones without requiring a separate authoritative DNS server.

**Business Value**

- Eliminates need for separate authoritative DNS server in small network environments
- Enables local zone hosting for internal domains without external DNS dependencies
- Supports split-horizon DNS architectures with internal and external zone views
- Provides zone transfer capability for secondary nameserver redundancy

**User Benefits**

- Network administrators can host internal DNS zones on the same infrastructure providing forwarding services
- Simplified DNS infrastructure reduces operational complexity and eliminates server proliferation
- Internal domains remain resolvable even if upstream internet connectivity fails

**Technical Context**

Authoritative DNS mode generates SOA (Start of Authority) records with configurable parameters: default TTL of 600 seconds (AUTH_TTL in `src/config.h` line 62), SOA refresh of 1200 seconds, SOA retry of 180 seconds, and SOA expiry of 1209600 seconds. The implementation supports A, AAAA, PTR, CNAME, MX, SRV, TXT, and NAPTR record types for authoritative zones, with per-zone subnet filtering and address exclusion lists.

#### 2.2.3.3 Dependencies

| Dependency Type | Description |
|----------------|-------------|
| **Prerequisite Features** | F-001 (DNS Forwarding and Caching) - shares DNS protocol handling |
| **System Dependencies** | Configuration defining authoritative zones and NS records |

| Dependency Type | Description |
|----------------|-------------|
| **External Dependencies** | None (implemented in core codebase) |
| **Integration Requirements** | Compile-time flag: HAVE_AUTH; configured auth zones and auth peers |

#### 2.2.3.4 Functional Requirements

## 2.3 DHCP Service Features

### 2.3.1 DHCPv4 Server (F-003)

#### 2.3.1.1 Feature Metadata

| Attribute | Value |
|-----------|-------|
| **Feature ID** | F-003 |
| **Feature Name** | DHCPv4 Server |
| **Category** | DHCP Services |
| **Priority** | Critical |

| Attribute | Value |
|-----------|-------|
| **Status** | Completed |
| **Complexity** | Medium |
| **Source Files** | `src/dhcp.c`, `src/rfc2131.c`, `src/lease.c`, `src/dhcp-protocol.h` |

#### 2.3.1.2 Description

**Overview**

The DHCPv4 Server provides complete DHCP server functionality conforming to RFC 2131, supporting both static lease reservations (binding specific MAC addresses to fixed IP addresses) and dynamic lease allocation from configured address pools. The implementation includes BOOTP protocol support, lease database persistence, automatic DNS integration, and comprehensive DHCP option handling.

**Business Value**

- Eliminates need for separate DHCP server deployment in small network environments
- Integrates seamlessly with DNS service to automatically register client hostnames
- Reduces administrative overhead through automatic lease-to-hostname synchronization
- Supports both legacy BOOTP clients and modern DHCPv4 protocol implementations

**User Benefits**

- Network administrators benefit from unified DNS-DHCP management eliminating configuration drift
- End users receive automatic network configuration without manual IP address assignment
- Dynamic hostname resolution enables name-based connectivity without static IP requirements
- PXE boot integration enables diskless workstation and thin client deployments

**Technical Context**

The DHCPv4 implementation handles the four-phase DHCP exchange (DISCOVER, OFFER, REQUEST, ACK) as defined in RFC 2131, with support for BOOTP compatibility, DHCPv4 rapid commit (RFC 4039), and DHCPv4 leasequery (added in v2.92). The system maintains a lease database with default location `/var/lib/misc/dnsmasq.leases` on Linux, supporting maximum 1000 concurrent leases (MAXLEASES in `src/config.h` line 40) with default lease time of 3600 seconds (DEFLEASE in `src/config.h` line 50).

### 2.3.2 DHCPv6 Server (F-004)

#### 2.3.2.1 Feature Metadata

| Attribute | Value |
|-----------|-------|
| **Feature ID** | F-004 |
| **Feature Name** | DHCPv6 Server |
| **Category** | DHCP Services |
| **Priority** | High |

| Attribute | Value |
|-----------|-------|
| **Status** | Completed |
| **Complexity** | Medium |
| **Source Files** | `src/dhcp6.c`, `src/rfc3315.c`, `src/dhcp6-protocol.h` |

#### 2.3.2.2 Description

**Overview**

The DHCPv6 Server implements stateful and stateless DHCPv6 operation modes per RFC 3315, providing IPv6 address and configuration parameter distribution to clients. The implementation coordinates with Router Advertisement to control whether clients use DHCPv6 for address assignment (stateful, M=1), configuration only (stateless, O=1), or SLAAC exclusively.

**Business Value**

- Enables centralized IPv6 address management in stateful mode with lease tracking
- Provides configuration parameters (DNS servers, domain search lists) in stateless mode while allowing SLAAC addressing
- Simplifies dual-stack network management through integrated IPv4 and IPv6 DHCP services
- Supports IPv6 prefix delegation for hierarchical network addressing

**User Benefits**

- Network administrators gain unified DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 management through single configuration
- IPv6 clients receive automatic network configuration matching operational mode (stateful/stateless)
- Coordinated operation with Router Advertisement eliminates manual client configuration

**Technical Context**

DHCPv6 implements the SOLICIT-ADVERTISE-REQUEST-REPLY message exchange for stateful operation and INFORMATION-REQUEST-REPLY for stateless operation. Default lease time is 86400 seconds (24 hours, DEFLEASE6 in `src/config.h` line 51), significantly longer than DHCPv4 due to IPv6 address abundance. The implementation integrates with F-005 (Router Advertisement) to set M (managed address) and O (other configuration) flags guiding client behavior.

#### 2.3.2.3 Dependencies

|----------------|-------------|
| **Prerequisite Features** | F-005 (IPv6 Router Advertisement) for client configuration mode coordination |
| **System Dependencies** | IPv6 kernel support, IPv6-enabled network interfaces |

| Dependency Type | Description |
|----------------|-------------|
| **External Dependencies** | None (implemented in core codebase) |
| **Integration Requirements** | Compile-time flag: HAVE_DHCP6 (implies HAVE_DHCP); F-001 for DHCPv6 hostname DNS integration |

| F-004-RQ-002 | Implement stateful DHCPv6 with address assignment and lease tracking | Must-Have |

| Requirement ID | Description | Priority |
|---------------|-------------|----------|
| F-004-RQ-003 | Implement stateless DHCPv6 providing configuration without addresses | Should-Have |
| F-004-RQ-004 | Coordinate with Router Advertisement for M and O flag configuration | Must-Have |

| Requirement ID | Description | Complexity |
|---------------|-------------|------------|
| F-004-RQ-005 | Support IPv6 prefix delegation for hierarchical networks | Medium |
| F-004-RQ-006 | Automatically register DHCPv6 client hostnames in DNS | Low |

**Detailed Requirements Table**

| Requirement ID | Acceptance Criteria | Performance Criteria |
|---------------|---------------------|---------------------|

### 2.3.3 IPv6 Router Advertisement and SLAAC (F-005)

#### 2.3.3.1 Feature Metadata

| Attribute | Value |
|-----------|-------|
| **Feature ID** | F-005 |
| **Feature Name** | IPv6 Router Advertisement and SLAAC |

|-----------|-------|
| **Status** | Completed |
| **Complexity** | Medium |
| **Source Files** | `src/radv.c`, `src/slaac.c`, `src/radv-protocol.h` |

#### 2.3.3.2 Description

**Overview**

IPv6 Router Advertisement broadcasts ICMPv6 Router Advertisement messages containing network configuration information to enable IPv6 Stateless Address Autoconfiguration (SLAAC). The implementation controls client address configuration behavior through M (managed) and O (other) flags, supports RDNSS (Recursive DNS Server) options, and coordinates with DHCPv6 for integrated IPv6 network management.

**Business Value**

- Enables zero-configuration IPv6 addressing through SLAAC without DHCP infrastructure
- Provides flexible deployment models: SLAAC-only, SLAAC+stateless DHCPv6, or full stateful DHCPv6
- Reduces administrative overhead through automatic client address configuration
- Supports prefix delegation for hierarchical IPv6 network architectures

**User Benefits**

- IPv6 clients receive automatic address configuration without manual setup
- Network administrators can choose appropriate IPv6 addressing model for their environment
- Coordinated DNS server distribution through RDNSS option eliminates separate DHCPv6 deployment for DNS-only needs

**Technical Context**

Router Advertisement implements ICMPv6 type 134 messages with prefix information options, M and O flags, and RDNSS options per RFC 4861 and RFC 6106. The implementation supports multiple operational modes: ra-only (SLAAC addressing, stateless DHCPv6 for configuration), ra-names (SLAAC with RDNSS), and ra-stateless (SLAAC addressing, no DHCPv6). Minimum RA lifetime is enforced at 2 hours to prevent rapid address changes.

| Requirement ID | Description | Priority |

## 2.4 Network Boot Features

### 2.4.1 Built-in TFTP Server (F-006)

#### 2.4.1.1 Feature Metadata

| Attribute | Value |
|-----------|-------|
| **Feature ID** | F-006 |
| **Feature Name** | Built-in TFTP Server |
| **Category** | Network Boot Services |
| **Priority** | High |

| Attribute | Value |
|-----------|-------|
| **Status** | Completed |
| **Complexity** | Low |
| **Source Files** | `src/tftp.c` |

#### 2.4.1.2 Description

**Overview**

The built-in TFTP Server provides read-only TFTP service primarily for network boot scenarios, supporting PXE boot, option negotiation for enhanced transfer performance, and secure root directory configuration. The implementation handles concurrent connections with configurable limits, supports multiple transfer modes, and integrates seamlessly with DHCP and PXE functionality.

**Business Value**

- Eliminates need for separate TFTP daemon in network boot environments
- Provides complete network boot infrastructure through DHCP-TFTP integration
- Reduces deployment complexity and administrative overhead for diskless workstation scenarios
- Enables secure boot file access through configurable root directories and permission checking

**User Benefits**

- Network administrators gain unified DHCP-TFTP-PXE infrastructure from single daemon
- PXE boot deployments simplified through integrated boot file serving and DHCP coordination
- Secure mode prevents unauthorized file access outside designated boot file directories

**Technical Context**

TFTP server implements RFC 1350 (basic TFTP) with option negotiation extensions per RFC 7440 (windowsize) and RFC 2349 (blksize, tsize, timeout). Maximum concurrent connections default to 50 (TFTP_MAX_CONNECTIONS in `src/config.h` line 54), maximum window size is 32 (TFTP_MAX_WINDOW in `src/config.h` line 55), and transfer timeout is 120 seconds (TFTP_TIMEOUT). The implementation supports netascii and binary (octet) transfer modes, with per-interface TFTP root directories and filename case conversion options.

| F-006-RQ-004 | Implement option negotiation for blksize, tsize, timeout, windowsize | Should-Have |

### 2.4.2 PXE Network Boot (F-007)

#### 2.4.2.1 Feature Metadata

| Attribute | Value |
|-----------|-------|
| **Feature ID** | F-007 |
| **Feature Name** | PXE Network Boot |
| **Category** | Network Boot Services |
| **Priority** | High |

| Attribute | Value |
|-----------|-------|
| **Status** | Completed |
| **Complexity** | Medium |
| **Source Files** | `src/dhcp.c`, `src/dhcp-protocol.h` (options 93, 175, PXE vendor-specific) |

#### 2.4.2.2 Description

**Overview**

PXE (Preboot Execution Environment) Network Boot provides network boot capabilities for diskless workstations, thin clients, and automated OS deployment systems. The implementation supports PXE proxy mode allowing coexistence with existing DHCP servers, multiple architecture detection, boot menu support, and integration with TFTP for boot file delivery.

**Business Value**

- Enables diskless workstation and thin client deployments without local storage requirements
- Supports automated OS deployment and system provisioning workflows
- Reduces hardware costs through centralized boot image management
- Provides flexible boot menu systems with multiple boot options per architecture

**User Benefits**

- IT administrators can deploy and manage diskless infrastructure from centralized boot servers
- PXE proxy mode enables network boot without replacing existing DHCP infrastructure
- Multi-architecture support handles heterogeneous client environments (x86, x86-64, IA64, EFI)
- Boot menu systems provide users with multiple OS or configuration choices at boot time

**Technical Context**

PXE implementation uses DHCP options for boot signaling: option 93 (client architecture type) identifies client platform, option 60 (vendor class) identifies PXE clients, option 67 (bootfile name) specifies boot image path, and option 175 (iPXE-specific options). Recent enhancement in v2.91 enables simultaneous PXE proxy-DHCP and DHCP relay operation, expanding deployment scenarios. PXE proxy mode allows dnsmasq to provide boot parameters without IP address assignment, coexisting with separate DHCP servers.

| **Prerequisite Features** | F-003 (DHCPv4 Server) for PXE-integrated DHCP, F-006 (TFTP Server) for boot file delivery |
| **System Dependencies** | PXE boot files in TFTP root directory, configured boot menu and architecture mappings |

| Dependency Type | Description |
|----------------|-------------|
| **External Dependencies** | None (implemented in core DHCP/TFTP codebase) |
| **Integration Requirements** | DHCP options 60, 67, 93, 175 configured; TFTP root contains boot images |

## 2.5 Integration Features

### 2.5.1 D-Bus Control Interface (F-009)

#### 2.5.1.1 Feature Metadata

| Attribute | Value |
|-----------|-------|
| **Feature ID** | F-009 |
| **Feature Name** | D-Bus Control Interface |
| **Category** | Integration Services |
| **Priority** | Low (platform-specific) |

| Attribute | Value |
|-----------|-------|
| **Status** | Completed |
| **Complexity** | Medium |
| **Source Files** | `src/dbus.c`, `dbus/dnsmasq.conf` (policy file) |

#### 2.5.1.2 Description

**Overview**

The D-Bus Control Interface exposes programmatic control and monitoring capabilities on the system bus, enabling external applications to query cache statistics, manipulate cache contents, retrieve configuration status, and reconfigure upstream DNS servers without daemon restart. The interface operates under the service name `uk.org.thekelleys.dnsmasq` with access control via system bus policy.

**Business Value**

- Enables integration with network management tools and monitoring systems
- Provides programmatic cache management for security tools and content filters
- Allows dynamic upstream server reconfiguration for VPN and network topology changes
- Reduces operational complexity through scriptable administrative operations

**User Benefits**

- System administrators can automate dnsmasq management through scripts and management tools
- Monitoring systems gain visibility into cache hit rates and query statistics
- Security tools can proactively clear cache entries for suspected compromised domains
- Network management tools can dynamically adjust DNS forwarding topology

**Technical Context**

D-Bus interface implemented in `src/dbus.c` using libdbus-1 library for system bus communication. System bus policy file `/etc/dbus-1/system.d/dnsmasq.conf` restricts interface access to root user and netadmin group members. Available D-Bus methods include cache query operations, cache clearing (SetServers reconfigures upstream servers, SetServersEx provides extended format), and configuration status retrieval. The interface operates on object path `/uk/org/thekelleys/dnsmasq`.

#### 2.5.1.3 Dependencies

| Dependency Type | Description |
|----------------|-------------|
| **Prerequisite Features** | F-001 (DNS Forwarding) - provides cache and upstream server management being exposed |
| **System Dependencies** | D-Bus system bus daemon running, policy file installed to `/etc/dbus-1/system.d/` |

| Dependency Type | Description |
|----------------|-------------|
| **External Dependencies** | libdbus-1 library for D-Bus communication |
| **Integration Requirements** | Compile-time flag: HAVE_DBUS; dnsmasq user must have D-Bus policy permissions |

#### 2.5.1.4 Functional Requirements

| F-009-RQ-002 | Expose D-Bus object at path `/uk/org/thekelleys/dnsmasq` | Must-Have |

| Requirement ID | Description | Priority |
|---------------|-------------|----------|
| F-009-RQ-003 | Provide method for querying DNS cache contents | Should-Have |
| F-009-RQ-004 | Provide method for clearing cache entries | Should-Have |

| Requirement ID | Description | Complexity |
|---------------|-------------|------------|
| F-009-RQ-005 | Provide SetServers method for upstream server reconfiguration | Medium |
| F-009-RQ-006 | Provide SetServersEx method for extended upstream configuration | Medium |

| Requirement ID | Description | Complexity |
|---------------|-------------|------------|

#### 2.5.2.2 Description

**Overview**

UBus Integration provides programmatic control interface for OpenWrt and embedded Linux distributions using UBus inter-process communication. The functionality parallels the D-Bus interface (F-009) but optimized for embedded systems with reduced memory footprint and simplified IPC mechanisms common in router and appliance firmware.

**Business Value**

- Enables integration with OpenWrt's LuCI web interface and system management tools
- Provides native IPC mechanism for embedded Linux distributions (LEDE, OpenWrt derivatives)
- Reduces memory overhead compared to D-Bus in resource-constrained environments
- Supports programmatic management matching embedded system operational patterns

**User Benefits**

- OpenWrt users gain web UI and CLI control of dnsmasq through native system interfaces
- Embedded system developers can integrate dnsmasq management into custom UIs
- Router manufacturers benefit from standardized management interface across OpenWrt ecosystem

**Technical Context**

UBus interface implemented in `src/ubus.c` using libubus library for UBus communication. Default service name is "dnsmasq" on the UBus system bus. The interface provides similar capabilities to D-Bus including cache query, upstream server reconfiguration, and lease information retrieval, but uses UBus's JSON-RPC-style message format and lightweight binary protocol optimized for embedded systems.

### 2.5.3 Firewall Integration (F-011)

#### 2.5.3.1 Feature Metadata

| Attribute | Value |
|-----------|-------|
| **Feature ID** | F-011 |
| **Feature Name** | Firewall Integration (ipset, nftables, PF, conntrack) |
| **Category** | Integration Services |
| **Priority** | Medium |

| Attribute | Value |
|-----------|-------|
| **Status** | Completed |
| **Complexity** | Medium |
| **Source Files** | `src/ipset.c`, `src/nftset.c`, `src/tables.c`, `src/conntrack.c` |

#### 2.5.3.2 Description

**Overview**

Firewall Integration enables dnsmasq to populate firewall data structures with resolved IP addresses, allowing dynamic firewall rule application based on DNS resolution results. The system supports multiple firewall technologies: Linux ipset (legacy and netlink APIs), Linux nftables sets, BSD PF (Packet Filter) tables, and Linux connection tracking mark preservation.

**Business Value**

- Enables domain-based firewall rules that automatically adapt as IP addresses change
- Supports content filtering and security policies based on DNS-level domain classification
- Reduces manual firewall rule maintenance for dynamic IP address spaces
- Provides foundation for advanced routing policies based on DNS resolution

**User Benefits**

- Network administrators can create firewall rules blocking or allowing entire domain categories
- Security tools can apply policies to dynamically resolved malware or advertising domains
- Advanced routing scenarios (policy-based routing, split tunneling) benefit from DNS-driven set population
- Eliminates manual tracking of IP addresses for frequently changing cloud services

**Technical Context**

Firewall integration operates at DNS query resolution time, adding resolved IP addresses to configured sets or tables immediately after successful resolution. Linux ipset integration (`src/ipset.c`) supports both legacy ipset API and modern netlink-based API. Linux nftables integration (`src/nftset.c`) requires libnftables library and populates named nftables sets in specified tables. BSD PF integration (`src/tables.c`) adds addresses to PF tables. Connection tracking integration (`src/conntrack.c`) preserves conntrack marks across NAT using libnetfilter_conntrack.

#### 2.5.3.3 Dependencies

|----------------|-------------|
| **Prerequisite Features** | F-001 (DNS Forwarding) - firewall sets populated from DNS resolution results |
| **System Dependencies** | Platform-specific firewall infrastructure: iptables+ipset (Linux), nftables (Linux), PF (BSD) |

| Dependency Type | Description |
|----------------|-------------|
| **External Dependencies** | Linux ipset (legacy or netlink), libnftables (nftables), libnetfilter_conntrack (conntrack) |
| **Integration Requirements** | Compile flags: HAVE_IPSET, HAVE_NFTSET, HAVE_CONNTRACK; firewall sets/tables pre-created |

#### 2.5.3.4 Functional Requirements

| F-011-RQ-002 | Add resolved IP addresses to nftables sets (Linux) | Should-Have |

| Requirement ID | Description | Priority |
|---------------|-------------|----------|
| F-011-RQ-003 | Add resolved IP addresses to PF tables (BSD) | Could-Have |
| F-011-RQ-004 | Preserve connection tracking marks across NAT (Linux) | Could-Have |

| Requirement ID | Description | Complexity |
|---------------|-------------|------------|
| F-011-RQ-005 | Support both legacy ipset API and netlink API | Medium |
| F-011-RQ-006 | Handle per-domain set/table configuration | Low |

### 2.5.4 Script Execution and Lua Integration (F-013)

#### 2.5.4.1 Feature Metadata

| Attribute | Value |
|-----------|-------|
| **Feature ID** | F-013 |
| **Feature Name** | Script Execution and Lua Integration |
| **Category** | Integration Services |
| **Priority** | Medium |

| Attribute | Value |
|-----------|-------|
| **Status** | Completed |
| **Complexity** | Medium |
| **Source Files** | `src/helper.c` |

#### 2.5.4.2 Description

**Overview**

Script Execution and Lua Integration enables external integration and automation through event-driven script execution on DHCP lease changes. The system supports both external script execution (fork-exec model) and embedded Lua scripting with reduced process overhead, passing lease details (MAC, IP, hostname, event type) to scripts for custom processing and integration workflows.

**Business Value**

- Enables integration with configuration management systems, monitoring tools, and custom workflows
- Supports dynamic DNS updates, firewall rule generation, and asset tracking based on DHCP events
- Reduces operational overhead through automated responses to network state changes
- Provides flexibility for site-specific customizations without modifying core daemon code

**User Benefits**

- System administrators can implement custom automation workflows triggered by lease events
- Dynamic DNS services can be updated automatically when devices obtain DHCP leases
- Asset management systems receive notifications of device network connections
- Firewall rules can be dynamically adjusted based on device identity (MAC address, hostname)

**Technical Context**

External script execution (`HAVE_SCRIPT` compile flag) uses fork-based helper processes managed by `src/helper.c`, executing configured script with action (add/old/del) and lease details as command-line arguments. Environment variables include DNSMASQ_LEASE_LENGTH, DNSMASQ_CLIENT_ID, DNSMASQ_INTERFACE, and other context. Lua scripting (`HAVE_LUASCRIPT` compile flag) embeds Lua interpreter for reduced process creation overhead, invoking Lua functions with same event triggers and data passing.

|----------------|-------------|
| **External Dependencies** | None for external scripts; Lua library for embedded Lua scripting |

| Requirement ID | Description | Priority |

| F-013-RQ-004 | Pass lease details as command-line arguments (action, MAC, IP, hostname) | Must-Have |

| Requirement ID | Description | Complexity |

| Requirement ID | Description | Complexity |

## 2.6 Platform and Support Features

### 2.6.1 Internationalized Domain Name (IDN) Support (F-012)

#### 2.6.1.1 Feature Metadata

| Attribute | Value |
|-----------|-------|
| **Feature ID** | F-012 |
| **Feature Name** | Internationalized Domain Name (IDN) Support |
| **Category** | Platform Support Features |
| **Priority** | Low (optional) |

| Attribute | Value |
|-----------|-------|
| **Status** | Completed |
| **Complexity** | Low |
| **Source Files** | IDN handling integrated throughout DNS modules |

#### 2.6.1.2 Description

**Overview**

Internationalized Domain Name (IDN) Support enables resolution of domain names containing non-ASCII characters (e.g., Chinese, Arabic, Cyrillic, emoji domains) by converting between Unicode representations and ASCII-Compatible Encoding (ACE) used in DNS protocol. The implementation supports both IDN 2003 (via libidn) and IDN 2008 (via libidn2) standards.

**Business Value**

- Enables DNS services for internationalized domain names in non-English speaking markets
- Supports global internet accessibility through native-language domain names
- Meets localization requirements for regional deployments
- Complies with modern IDN standards (IDN 2008) while maintaining backward compatibility (IDN 2003)

**User Benefits**

- Users can access websites with native-language domain names without manual ASCII conversion
- Network administrators can resolve both legacy IDN 2003 and modern IDN 2008 domains
- Improved accessibility for non-English speaking user communities

**Technical Context**

IDN support is implemented through optional external libraries: libidn for IDN 2003 (HAVE_IDN compile flag, Makefile lines 58-59) or libidn2 for IDN 2008 (HAVE_LIBIDN2 compile flag, Makefile lines 60-61). The libraries handle Punycode encoding/decoding and Unicode normalization, with dnsmasq converting between UTF-8 configuration input and ACE format for DNS wire protocol.

#### 2.6.1.3 Dependencies

| Dependency Type | Description |
|----------------|-------------|
| **Prerequisite Features** | F-001 (DNS Forwarding) - IDN conversion applied to DNS queries |
| **System Dependencies** | None beyond IDN library |

| Dependency Type | Description |
|----------------|-------------|
| **External Dependencies** | libidn (IDN 2003) OR libidn2 (IDN 2008) - mutually exclusive options |
| **Integration Requirements** | Compile flag: HAVE_IDN or HAVE_LIBIDN2; library detected via pkg-config |

#### 2.6.1.4 Functional Requirements

| Requirement ID | Description | Priority |
|---------------|-------------|----------|
| F-012-RQ-001 | Convert Unicode domain names to ACE for DNS wire protocol | Must-Have |
| F-012-RQ-002 | Convert ACE responses back to Unicode for logging/display | Should-Have |

| Requirement ID | Description | Complexity |
|---------------|-------------|------------|
| F-012-RQ-003 | Support IDN 2003 via libidn library | Low |
| F-012-RQ-004 | Support IDN 2008 via libidn2 library | Low |

**Detailed Requirements Table**

| Requirement ID | Acceptance Criteria | Performance Criteria |
|---------------|---------------------|---------------------|
| F-012-RQ-001 | Unicode domain names converted to xn-- ACE format for DNS queries | Conversion latency <1ms per domain |
| F-012-RQ-002 | ACE domains displayed as Unicode in logs when logging enabled | Display conversion for log output only |
| F-012-RQ-003 | IDN 2003 domains (e.g., German eszett) handled correctly with libidn | Punycode encoding per RFC 3490 |
| F-012-RQ-004 | IDN 2008 domains handled per IDNA2008 specification with libidn2 | IDNA2008 compliance per RFC 5891 |

**Validation Rules**

| Requirement ID | Business Rules | Compliance Requirements |
|---------------|----------------|----------------------|
| F-012-RQ-001 | Only valid Unicode characters allowed in domain names | Library performs validation |
| F-012-RQ-003 | IDN 2003 and IDN 2008 mutually exclusive (single library used) | RFC 3490 (IDN 2003) |
| F-012-RQ-004 | IDN 2008 preferred for new deployments | RFC 5891 (IDNA2008) |

### 2.6.2 Platform-Specific Integration (F-014)

#### 2.6.2.1 Feature Metadata

| Attribute | Value |
|-----------|-------|

#### 2.6.2.2 Description

**Overview**

Platform-Specific Integration provides native service management, configuration persistence, and system integration for diverse operating systems including Linux, BSD variants, macOS, Solaris, and Android. The implementation adapts to platform-specific APIs (netlink for Linux, BPF for BSD), service managers (systemd, launchd, SMF), and configuration storage mechanisms (filesystem, nvram).

**Business Value**

- Ensures native operating system integration on all supported platforms
- Enables deployment in heterogeneous environments without requiring platform abstraction layers
- Provides optimized performance through platform-specific API usage
- Supports embedded systems with specialized storage (nvram) and memory constraints

**User Benefits**

- Users experience native service management on their platform (systemd, launchd, etc.)
- Platform-specific optimizations improve performance and reduce resource usage
- Consistent functionality across operating systems simplifies cross-platform deployments

**Technical Context**

Platform-specific code isolated in dedicated modules and contrib utilities. Linux uses netlink interface monitoring (`src/netlink.c`), BSD uses Berkeley Packet Filter (`src/bpf.c`), Android includes AOSP build system integration (`bld/Android.mk`), macOS provides launchd service manager (`contrib/MacOSX-launchd/`), Solaris offers SMF integration (`contrib/Solaris10/`), and WRT routers support nvram-based lease persistence (`contrib/wrt/`). Platform file paths configured in `src/config.h` lines 207-243.

### 2.6.3 Monitoring and Logging (F-015)

#### 2.6.3.1 Feature Metadata

| Attribute | Value |
|-----------|-------|
| **Feature ID** | F-015 |
| **Feature Name** | Monitoring and Logging |
| **Category** | Platform Support Features |
| **Priority** | Medium |

| Attribute | Value |
|-----------|-------|
| **Status** | Completed |
| **Complexity** | Low |
| **Source Files** | `src/log.c`, `src/metrics.c`, `src/metrics.h` |

#### 2.6.3.2 Description

**Overview**

Monitoring and Logging provides operational visibility into DNS queries, DHCP transactions, cache statistics, and system events through syslog integration and signal-triggered statistics dumps. The implementation uses non-blocking, fork-safe logging to prevent performance degradation and supports configurable log levels for troubleshooting and audit purposes.

**Business Value**

- Enables operational troubleshooting through detailed query and transaction logging
- Provides visibility into cache effectiveness and performance metrics
- Supports security auditing and compliance requirements through query logging
- Facilitates capacity planning through statistics collection

**User Benefits**

- System administrators gain visibility into DNS resolution patterns and DHCP activity
- Troubleshooting capabilities through detailed query logging and error reporting
- Performance monitoring through cache hit rate statistics
- Security teams can audit DNS queries for suspicious activity

**Technical Context**

Logging system (`src/log.c`) implements non-blocking, fork-safe logging queue (LOG_MAX=5) that prevents logging operations from blocking the main event loop. Syslog integration uses daemon facility for log messages. Query logging enabled via `--log-queries` option, DHCP transaction logging via `--log-dhcp`. Cache statistics generated on SIGUSR1 signal. Basic metrics collection in `src/metrics.c` and `src/metrics.h` provides cache hit/miss counters and query rate tracking.

#### 2.6.3.3 Dependencies

| Dependency Type | Description |
|----------------|-------------|
| **Prerequisite Features** | F-001 (DNS) and F-003 (DHCP) generate events for logging |
| **System Dependencies** | Syslog daemon for log message delivery |

| Dependency Type | Description |
|----------------|-------------|
| **External Dependencies** | None (uses standard syslog API) |
| **Integration Requirements** | Syslog daemon configured to receive daemon facility messages |

#### 2.6.3.4 Functional Requirements

| Requirement ID | Description | Priority |
|---------------|-------------|----------|
| F-015-RQ-001 | Log messages to syslog daemon facility | Must-Have |
| F-015-RQ-002 | Implement non-blocking logging queue to prevent main loop blocking | Must-Have |

| Requirement ID | Description | Priority |
|---------------|-------------|----------|
| F-015-RQ-003 | Log DNS queries when query logging enabled (--log-queries) | Should-Have |
| F-015-RQ-004 | Log DHCP transactions when DHCP logging enabled (--log-dhcp) | Should-Have |

| Requirement ID | Description | Complexity |
|---------------|-------------|------------|
| F-015-RQ-005 | Generate cache statistics on SIGUSR1 signal | Low |
| F-015-RQ-006 | Track cache hit/miss ratios and query rates | Low |

**Detailed Requirements Table**

| Requirement ID | Acceptance Criteria | Performance Criteria |
|---------------|---------------------|---------------------|
| F-015-RQ-001 | Log messages appear in syslog (typically /var/log/daemon.log or journalctl) | Logging latency does not block query processing |
| F-015-RQ-002 | Logging queue depth limited to 5 entries; queue full drops messages with warning | Queue processing adds <0.1ms latency |
| F-015-RQ-003 | Each DNS query logged with timestamp, client IP, query name, query type | Query logging adds <1ms latency |
| F-015-RQ-004 | DHCP transactions logged with MAC, IP, hostname, lease time | DHCP logging adds <1ms latency |

| Requirement ID | Input Parameters | Output/Response |
|---------------|------------------|----------------|
| F-015-RQ-003 | Query logging enabled, DNS query details | Syslog message: "query[A] example.com from 192.168.1.10" |
| F-015-RQ-004 | DHCP logging enabled, DHCP transaction | Syslog message: "DHCPACK(eth0) 192.168.1.100 00:11:22:33:44:55 hostname" |
| F-015-RQ-005 | SIGUSR1 signal sent to dnsmasq process | Cache statistics written to syslog |
| F-015-RQ-006 | Cache operations (hits, misses) | Counters incremented, available for statistics dump |

**Validation Rules**

| Requirement ID | Business Rules | Security Requirements |
|---------------|----------------|---------------------|
| F-015-RQ-002 | Queue full condition logged to prevent silent log loss | Log queue size configurable in future versions |
| F-015-RQ-003 | Query logging may impact performance under high load | Disabled by default for performance |
| F-015-RQ-004 | DHCP logging reveals client MAC addresses and hostnames | Privacy considerations for log retention |

- **Extensions**: F-005 (Router Advertisement for IPv6 coordination), F-016 (Advanced DHCP features)

**Network Boot Cluster:**
- **Primary**: F-006 (TFTP Server), F-007 (PXE Boot)

- **Monitoring**: F-015 (Logging and statistics)

### 2.7.4 Integration Points

**DNS-DHCP Integration:**
- DHCP lease hostnames automatically registered in DNS cache (F-003/F-004 → F-001)
- DHCP clients immediately resolvable by hostname without manual DNS configuration
- Lease expiration triggers DNS cache entry removal

**DHCP-Network Boot Integration:**
- DHCPv4 provides PXE boot parameters via options 60, 67, 93 (F-003 → F-007)
- TFTP server delivers boot images specified in DHCP options (F-007 → F-006)
- PXE proxy mode enables coexistence with existing DHCP infrastructure

**DHCPv6-Router Advertisement Coordination:**
- Router Advertisement M/O flags control DHCPv6 behavior (F-005 ↔ F-004)
- M=1: Stateful DHCPv6 with address assignment
- O=1: Stateless DHCPv6 with configuration only
- M=O=0: SLAAC-only with no DHCPv6

**DNS-Firewall Integration:**
- Resolved IP addresses dynamically populate firewall sets/tables (F-001 → F-011)
- Enables domain-based firewall rules that adapt to IP changes
- Supports content filtering and policy-based routing

## 2.8 Implementation Considerations

### 2.8.1 Technical Constraints

#### 2.8.1.1 Performance Limits

The following performance limits are enforced to prevent resource exhaustion and denial-of-service attacks:

| Constraint | Default Limit | Configuration Source | Rationale |
|-----------|---------------|---------------------|-----------|
| DNS cache size | 150 entries | `CACHESIZ` (config.h:38) | Balances memory usage vs. hit rate |
| Outstanding DNS requests | 150 queries | `FTABSIZ` (config.h:17) | Limits concurrent query state |

| Constraint | Default Limit | Configuration Source | Rationale |
|-----------|---------------|---------------------|-----------|
| TCP child processes | 20 | `MAX_PROCS` (config.h:18) | Prevents TCP connection flooding |
| TCP queries per connection | 100 | `TCP_MAX_QUERIES` (config.h:20) | Limits per-connection resource usage |

| Constraint | Default Limit | Configuration Source | Rationale |
|-----------|---------------|---------------------|-----------|
| DHCP maximum leases | 1000 | `MAXLEASES` (config.h:40) | Suitable for small network scale |
| TFTP max connections | 50 | `TFTP_MAX_CONNECTIONS` (config.h:54) | Balances boot concurrency vs. resources |

| Constraint | Default Limit | Configuration Source | Rationale |
|-----------|---------------|---------------------|-----------|
| DNSSEC queries per validation | 40 | `DNSSEC_LIMIT_WORK` (config.h:25) | Prevents validation DoS |
| DNSSEC signature failures | 20 | `DNSSEC_LIMIT_SIG_FAIL` (config.h:26) | Limits crypto operations |

| Constraint | Default Limit | Configuration Source | Rationale |
|-----------|---------------|---------------------|-----------|
| DNSSEC crypto operations | 200 | `DNSSEC_LIMIT_CRYPTO` (config.h:27) | CPU resource protection |
| NSEC3 iterations | 150 | `DNSSEC_LIMIT_NSEC3_ITERS` (config.h:29) | Computational complexity limit |

#### 2.8.1.2 Scalability Considerations

**Target Deployment Scale:**
- **Client Count**: 100-250 concurrent clients (typical small network)
- **Query Rate**: Hundreds to low thousands of queries per second
- **Lease Churn**: Dozens of lease assignments per minute
- **Configuration Size**: Thousands of static host entries and DHCP reservations
- **Interface Count**: Dozens of monitored network interfaces

**Scaling Limitations:**
- Single-threaded architecture limits CPU utilization to one core
- Fixed-size data structures (cache, lease table) constrain maximum capacity
- Memory consumption grows linearly with cache size and lease count
- Not suitable for enterprise-scale deployments (thousands of clients, tens of thousands QPS)

**Performance Optimization Strategies:**
- Cache size tuning: Increase `--cache-size` for larger deployments (supports thousands of entries)
- Negative caching: Reduces upstream load during DNS failures
- DHCP lease time tuning: Longer leases reduce transaction rate
- Query timeout configuration: Balance responsiveness vs. upstream server patience

#### 2.8.1.3 Resource Consumption Targets

| Resource | Target Range | Factors |
|----------|-------------|---------|
| **Memory (RSS)** | 1-10 MB | Cache size, lease count, configuration size |
| **Storage (binary)** | <100 KB (embedded, stripped) | Compile-time feature selection |

| Resource | Target Range | Factors |
|----------|-------------|---------|
| **CPU Utilization** | <5% (single core, idle) | Query rate, DNSSEC validation load |
| **Disk I/O** | Minimal (async lease writes) | DHCP lease churn rate |

### 2.8.2 Security Implications

#### 2.8.2.1 Privilege Separation

**Implementation:**
- Daemon starts as root to bind privileged ports (53, 67, 69)
- Drops privileges to configured unprivileged user (default "nobody", group "dip") after initialization
- Configurable via `--user` option

**Rationale:**
- Minimizes attack surface by running bulk of processing with minimal privileges
- Compromised daemon cannot directly modify system configuration or access protected resources
- Follows principle of least privilege

#### 2.8.2.2 DNSSEC Security

**Protection Against:**
- DNS cache poisoning: Cryptographic validation prevents forged responses
- Man-in-the-middle attacks: Signature verification ensures response authenticity
- Domain hijacking: Trust chain validation from root zone to target domain

**Implementation Details:**
- Trust anchor validation against `trust-anchors.conf` (root zone KSK)
- Complete validation chain: RRSIG → DNSKEY → DS → parent zone
- Bogus response handling: Return SERVFAIL, do not cache invalid data
- Resource limits prevent DNSSEC validation DoS attacks

#### 2.8.2.3 TFTP Security

**Secure Mode:**
- File ownership verification: Only serve files owned by dnsmasq user
- Root directory restriction: Path traversal prevention
- Read-only operation: No file upload capability

**Deployment Considerations:**
- Boot files should have restrictive permissions (644, owned by dnsmasq user)
- TFTP root should be separate from general filesystem
- Consider separate VLAN or network segment for PXE boot traffic

#### 2.8.2.4 Access Control

**D-Bus Interface:**
- System bus policy restricts access to root and netadmin group
- Policy file: `/etc/dbus-1/system.d/dnsmasq.conf`
- Prevents unprivileged users from manipulating cache or configuration

**Script Execution:**
- Lease-change scripts execute as unprivileged daemon user
- Hostname and argument sanitization prevents shell injection
- Script execution failures logged but non-fatal

### 2.8.3 Maintenance Requirements

#### 2.8.3.1 Configuration Reload

**Hot Reload Capability:**
- SIGHUP signal triggers configuration reload without daemon restart
- DNS cache cleared and repopulated
- DHCP leases preserved across reload
- Active DNS queries and DHCP transactions complete correctly

**Use Cases:**
- Adding/removing static host entries
- Adjusting upstream DNS servers
- Modifying DHCP pools and options
- Updating firewall integration configuration

#### 2.8.3.2 DNSSEC Trust Anchor Maintenance

**Trust Anchor Updates:**
- Root zone KSK changes require `trust-anchors.conf` update
- Current trust anchors valid as of July 2024
- Monitor IANA announcements for KSK rollovers
- Automated trust anchor update mechanisms (RFC 5011) not currently implemented

**Validation:**
- Test DNSSEC validation after trust anchor update
- Monitor logs for validation failures
- Verify queries to signed zones return validated responses

#### 2.8.3.3 Lease Database Maintenance

**Lease File Management:**
- Location: `/var/lib/misc/dnsmasq.leases` (Linux default)
- Format: Text file, one lease per line
- Persistence: Leases survive daemon restart
- Corruption handling: Validation on load, graceful degradation

**Backup Considerations:**
- Lease file should be included in system backups
- Corruption recovery: Delete lease file, daemon starts with empty database
- Lease expiration cleanup: Daemon automatically removes expired leases

#### 2.8.3.4 Log Management

**Syslog Integration:**
- Messages sent to syslog daemon facility
- Log rotation handled by syslog/logrotate configuration
- Query logging volume can be substantial under high load

**Log Retention:**
- Query logs may contain privacy-sensitive information (hostnames, IP addresses)
- DHCP logs reveal device identities (MAC addresses, hostnames)
- Compliance requirements may dictate retention periods
- Consider log anonymization for long-term retention
