## 6.5 Monitoring and Observability

### 6.5.1 Monitoring Philosophy and Architectural Approach

#### 6.5.1.1 Design Principles

Dnsmasq implements a **lightweight Unix philosophy approach** to monitoring and observability, fundamentally different from modern microservices observability platforms. The system prioritizes minimal resource overhead, operational simplicity, and standard Unix integration over sophisticated built-in dashboards, alerting, or distributed tracing capabilities.

**Core Design Principles**:

- **Raw Data Export**: Provide comprehensive operational data (metrics, logs, cache state) through simple interfaces; delegate interpretation, aggregation, and alerting to external systems
- **Standard Integration Points**: Use universal Unix/Linux interfaces (syslog, D-Bus, signals, UBus) that integrate naturally with existing system monitoring infrastructure
- **Non-Blocking Operations**: All monitoring data collection mechanisms are designed to never introduce latency into DNS/DHCP packet processing paths
- **Zero Default Overhead**: Metrics collection uses simple counter increments; verbose logging is opt-in; no always-on distributed tracing
- **Embedded-Friendly**: Monitoring infrastructure consumes minimal memory and CPU, suitable for devices with 8-16MB RAM

**Architectural Positioning**:

This monitoring architecture targets **small network deployments** (home networks, small offices, embedded devices) where dedicated observability platforms (Prometheus, Grafana, ELK Stack, distributed tracing) may not exist. Operators rely on syslog, shell scripts, and manual introspection for troubleshooting rather than automated incident response workflows.

For **enterprise-grade observability** (SLA tracking, automated alerting, performance dashboards, anomaly detection), dnsmasq requires integration with external monitoring systems that consume metrics via D-Bus/UBus APIs and logs via syslog aggregation.

#### 6.5.1.2 Scope and Limitations

**What Dnsmasq Provides**:

- ✅ Comprehensive operational metrics (30+ counters) tracking DNS and DHCP subsystem activity
- ✅ Per-upstream-server performance metrics (queries, failures, latency)
- ✅ Detailed syslog integration with configurable verbosity levels
- ✅ Signal-based cache introspection and statistics dumps
- ✅ D-Bus/UBus programmatic access to metrics and control functions
- ✅ PCAP packet dumping for deep protocol troubleshooting

**What Dnsmasq Does NOT Provide**:

- ❌ **No Built-In Dashboards**: No web UI, no real-time visualizations, no embedded graphs
- ❌ **No Alerting System**: Never generates alerts, emails, webhook calls, or pages on-call engineers
- ❌ **No Distributed Tracing**: Single-threaded architecture with no OpenTelemetry, Jaeger, or Zipkin integration
- ❌ **No Automated SLA Tracking**: Does not measure response time percentiles, uptime percentages, or SLA compliance automatically
- ❌ **No Historical Time-Series Storage**: Metrics are point-in-time counters only; no built-in trend analysis
- ❌ **No Anomaly Detection**: No machine learning, pattern recognition, or predictive analytics

**Design Rationale**:

Section 1.2.2.3 of the Technical Specification documents that dnsmasq's target deployments include embedded routers with single-core ARM processors and minimal RAM. Sophisticated observability platforms would consume more resources than the core DNS/DHCP services themselves. The lightweight approach enables operation in resource-constrained environments while providing sufficient data for external monitoring when needed.

### 6.5.2 Monitoring Infrastructure

#### 6.5.2.1 Metrics Collection System

##### 6.5.2.1.1 Implementation Architecture

The metrics subsystem (`src/metrics.c`, `src/metrics.h`) implements a **simple counter array** stored in the global daemon structure. Metrics collection introduces **zero overhead** beyond single-instruction counter increments at event points throughout the codebase.

```c
// Metrics storage in daemon structure (src/dnsmasq.h line 1292)
struct daemon {
    // ... other fields ...
    unsigned int metrics[__METRIC_MAX];  // Fixed-size counter array
    // ... other fields ...
};

// Counter increment at event points (src/forward.c, src/dhcp.c, etc.)
daemon->metrics[METRIC_DNS_QUERIES_FORWARDED]++;
daemon->metrics[METRIC_DHCP_ACK]++;
```

**Architectural Characteristics**:

- **In-Memory Only**: No persistent storage; counters reset on process restart
- **Monotonic Counters**: Values only increase, never decrease (except on explicit reset or overflow)
- **Non-Blocking**: Counter increments are atomic single-instruction operations with no locking
- **Fixed Capacity**: Exactly 30 global metrics (enumerated in `src/metrics.h` lines 18-50)
- **Per-Server Tracking**: Additional per-upstream-server metrics tracked separately in `struct server`

##### 6.5.2.1.2 Global Metrics Catalog

**DNS Operation Metrics** (9 metrics):

| Metric Name | Description | Increment Location | Operational Significance |
|-------------|-------------|-------------------|-------------------------|
| `METRIC_DNS_CACHE_INSERTED` | Total cache insertions | `src/cache.c` on upstream response | Indicates query volume and cache churn |
| `METRIC_DNS_CACHE_LIVE_FREED` | Cache entries evicted while still valid (LRU) | `src/cache.c` on eviction | High values indicate cache pressure |
| `METRIC_DNS_QUERIES_FORWARDED` | Queries sent to upstream servers | `src/forward.c` on query transmission | Measures cache miss rate |
| `METRIC_DNS_AUTH_ANSWERED` | Authoritative zone responses | `src/auth.c` on auth reply | Tracks local zone usage |
| `METRIC_DNS_LOCAL_ANSWERED` | Queries answered from cache/hosts | `src/cache.c` on cache hit | Measures cache effectiveness |
| `METRIC_DNS_STALE_ANSWERED` | Stale cache entries served | `src/forward.c` on stale serve | Indicates upstream unavailability |
| `METRIC_DNS_UNANSWERED_QUERY` | Queries with no valid response | `src/forward.c` on failure | Error rate indicator |
| `METRIC_CRYPTO_HWM` | Max concurrent DNSSEC crypto operations | `src/dnssec.c` on validation | DNSSEC load high water mark |
| `METRIC_SIG_FAIL_HWM` | Max signature validation failures per query | `src/dnssec.c` on validation failure | DNSSEC complexity indicator |

**DHCP Transaction Metrics** (12 metrics):

| Metric Name | Description | Increment Location | Operational Significance |
|-------------|-------------|-------------------|-------------------------|
| `METRIC_BOOTP` | BOOTP requests processed | `src/dhcp.c` on BOOTP | Legacy client detection |
| `METRIC_PXE` | PXE boot requests | `src/dhcp.c` on PXE | Network boot activity |
| `METRIC_DHCPACK` | DHCPACK messages sent | `src/dhcp.c` on ACK | Successful lease assignments |
| `METRIC_DHCPDECLINE` | DHCPDECLINE received | `src/dhcp.c` on DECLINE | IP conflict indicator |
| `METRIC_DHCPDISCOVER` | DHCPDISCOVER received | `src/dhcp.c` on DISCOVER | New client requests |
| `METRIC_DHCPINFORM` | DHCPINFORM received | `src/dhcp.c` on INFORM | Configuration-only requests |
| `METRIC_DHCPNAK` | DHCPNAK sent | `src/dhcp.c` on NAK | Rejected lease requests |
| `METRIC_DHCPOFFER` | DHCPOFFER sent | `src/dhcp.c` on OFFER | Available address responses |
| `METRIC_DHCPREQUEST` | DHCPREQUEST received | `src/dhcp.c` on REQUEST | Lease confirmations |
| `METRIC_DHCPRELEASE` | DHCPRELEASE received | `src/dhcp.c` on RELEASE | Voluntary lease terminations |
| `METRIC_NOANSWER` | No address available | `src/dhcp.c` on exhaustion | **Pool exhaustion critical alert** |
| `METRIC_LEASES_ALLOCATED_4/6` | IPv4/IPv6 leases created | `src/lease.c` on allocation | Capacity utilization |

**Connection and Capacity Metrics** (9 metrics):

| Metric Name | Description | Update Location | Operational Significance |
|-------------|-------------|----------------|-------------------------|
| `METRIC_TCP_CONNECTIONS` | Current TCP connection count | `src/forward.c` on connect/disconnect | Real-time load indicator |
| `METRIC_LEASES_PRUNED_4/6` | Expired/deleted leases | `src/lease.c` on expiration | Lease churn rate |
| `METRIC_DHCPLEASEQUERY` | DHCPv4 lease query messages | `src/dhcp.c` on query | Lease information requests |
| `METRIC_DHCPLEASEUNASSIGNED` | Unassigned lease query responses | `src/dhcp.c` on query result | Available address queries |
| `METRIC_DHCPLEASEACTIVE` | Active lease query responses | `src/dhcp.c` on query result | Allocated address queries |
| `METRIC_DHCPLEASEUNKNOWN` | Unknown lease query responses | `src/dhcp.c` on query result | Invalid query responses |
| `METRIC_WORK_HWM` | Max DNSSEC subqueries per client query | `src/dnssec.c` on validation | DNSSEC query amplification |

##### 6.5.2.1.3 Per-Upstream-Server Metrics

Each configured upstream DNS server maintains a dedicated metrics structure (`struct server` in `src/dnsmasq.h` lines 830-870):

```c
struct server {
    // ... connection details ...
    unsigned int queries;           // Total queries sent to this server
    unsigned int failed_queries;    // Queries that failed or timed out
    unsigned int retrys;           // Query retry count
    unsigned int nxdomain_replies; // NXDOMAIN responses from this server
    unsigned int query_latency;    // Cumulative latency for average calculation
    // ... other fields ...
};
```

**Latency Calculation**:

Average latency is computed by tracking cumulative query latency and dividing by successful query count. Implementation in `src/forward.c` measures time between query transmission and response reception:

```c
// Pseudo-code representation
server->queries_sent = current_time_milliseconds();
send_query_to_upstream(server, query);
// ... wait for response ...
latency_ms = current_time_milliseconds() - server->queries_sent;
server->query_latency += latency_ms;
average_latency = server->query_latency / server->queries;
```

**Upstream Health Tracking**:

The DNS forwarder uses failure counters to implement **automatic upstream failover** (Section 5.4.2.1 Error Handling Strategy). After multiple consecutive failures (typically 3-5), a server is marked as "failed" and receives lower selection priority. Periodic health checks every 20 seconds (FORWARD_TIME constant in `src/config.h`) probe failed servers to detect recovery.

#### 6.5.2.2 Metrics Access Methods

##### 6.5.2.2.1 D-Bus Interface (Optional: HAVE_DBUS)

**Service Registration**: `uk.org.thekelleys.dnsmasq` on system bus  
**Object Path**: `/uk/org/thekelleys/dnsmasq`  
**Implementation**: `src/dbus.c` lines 690-903

**Available Methods**:

**GetMetrics() → a{su}**

Returns all global metrics as a dictionary mapping metric names to uint32 values:

```python
# Python example using python-dbus
import dbus

bus = dbus.SystemBus()
proxy = bus.get_object('uk.org.thekelleys.dnsmasq', '/uk/org/thekelleys/dnsmasq')
dnsmasq = dbus.Interface(proxy, 'uk.org.thekelleys.dnsmasq')

metrics = dnsmasq.GetMetrics()
print(f"DNS Cache Hits: {metrics['dns_local_answered']}")
print(f"DNS Cache Misses: {metrics['dns_queries_forwarded']}")
print(f"DHCP Pool Exhaustion: {metrics['noanswer']}")
```

**GetServerMetrics() → aa{ss}**

Returns per-upstream-server statistics as an array of dictionaries:

```python
servers = dnsmasq.GetServerMetrics()
for server in servers:
    print(f"Server: {server['address']}:{server['port']}")
    print(f"  Queries: {server['queries']}, Failed: {server['failed_queries']}")
    print(f"  NXDOMAIN: {server['nxdomain']}, Retries: {server['retries']}")
    print(f"  Average Latency: {server['latency']}ms")
```

**ClearMetrics() → void**

Resets all global metrics and per-server counters to zero:

```bash
# Command-line invocation
dbus-send --system --dest=uk.org.thekelleys.dnsmasq \
  /uk/org/thekelleys/dnsmasq \
  uk.org.thekelleys.dnsmasq.ClearMetrics
```

**Security Enforcement**:

D-Bus access controlled by `/etc/dbus-1/system.d/dnsmasq.conf` policy file restricting administrative methods to root user only. Unauthorized access attempts return `org.freedesktop.DBus.Error.AccessDenied`.

##### 6.5.2.2.2 UBus Interface (Optional: HAVE_UBUS)

**Purpose**: Lightweight monitoring interface for OpenWrt and embedded Linux systems using UBus instead of D-Bus

**Service Name**: Configurable via `--ubus-name` option (default: `dnsmasq`)  
**Implementation**: `src/ubus.c` lines 184-201

**Available Methods**:

**metrics** → UBus table with key-value pairs

```bash
# Command-line invocation (OpenWrt)
ubus call dnsmasq metrics
{
    "dns_cache_inserted": 15234,
    "dns_queries_forwarded": 8912,
    "dns_local_answered": 6322,
    "dhcp_ack": 42,
    "noanswer": 0
}
```

**Limitation**: UBus interface provides only global metrics; per-server metrics (equivalent to D-Bus GetServerMetrics) are NOT available via UBus.

##### 6.5.2.2.3 Signal-Based Cache Dump (SIGUSR1)

**Trigger Mechanism**: Send SIGUSR1 to dnsmasq process

```bash
kill -USR1 $(cat /var/run/dnsmasq.pid)
# or
killall -USR1 dnsmasq
# or via systemd
systemctl kill --signal=SIGUSR1 dnsmasq
```

**Implementation**: `src/cache.c:dump_cache()` function (lines 2063-2128)

**Output Destination**: Syslog with LOG_INFO facility

**Information Included**:

1. **Timestamp**: Current Unix timestamp
2. **Cache Statistics**:
   - Configured cache size
   - Cache insertions vs. LRU evictions (cache efficiency indicator)
   - Queries forwarded vs. answered locally (cache hit ratio)
   - Stale cache responses served (upstream failure indicator)
   - Authoritative zone responses (if `--auth-zone` configured)
3. **DNSSEC High Water Marks** (if HAVE_DNSSEC enabled):
   - Maximum concurrent DNSSEC subqueries
   - Maximum cryptographic operations
   - Maximum signature validation failures
4. **TCP Connection Statistics**:
   - Current TCP connections
   - Peak TCP connections since last SIGUSR1
   - Configured maximum (MAX_PROCS limit)
5. **Per-Upstream-Server Statistics**:
   - Server address and port
   - Queries sent, retries, failures, NXDOMAIN count
   - Average latency in milliseconds
6. **Complete Cache Contents** (if `--log-queries` or `--debug` enabled):
   - Every cached entry with hostname, IP, TTL, expiration time, source

**Example Syslog Output**:

```
Nov  5 10:30:15 router dnsmasq[1234]: time 1730806215
Nov  5 10:30:15 router dnsmasq[1234]: cache size 150, 12/156 cache insertions re-used unexpired cache entries.
Nov  5 10:30:15 router dnsmasq[1234]: queries forwarded 892, queries answered locally 1534
Nov  5 10:30:15 router dnsmasq[1234]: queries for authoritative zones 45
Nov  5 10:30:15 router dnsmasq[1234]: server 8.8.8.8#53: queries sent 450, retried 5, failed 2, nxdomain replies 12, avg. latency 25ms
Nov  5 10:30:15 router dnsmasq[1234]: server 1.1.1.1#53: queries sent 442, retried 3, failed 1, nxdomain replies 15, avg. latency 18ms
Nov  5 10:30:15 router dnsmasq[1234]: TCP active connections 3, maximum since last dump 7, max limit 20
```

**Use Cases**:

- **Periodic Monitoring**: cron job triggers SIGUSR1 every 5 minutes, parses syslog for metrics
- **Incident Response**: Manual statistics collection during troubleshooting
- **Capacity Planning**: Analyze cache efficiency and upstream server performance trends
- **Configuration Validation**: Verify upstream servers are responding correctly after configuration changes

#### 6.5.2.3 Log Aggregation System

##### 6.5.2.3.1 Asynchronous Logging Architecture

**Implementation**: `src/log.c` (495 lines)

**Design Problem Solved**:

If syslog daemon is slow or blocked (e.g., making DNS queries back through dnsmasq, creating circular dependency), synchronous logging would block the main event loop and introduce latency into DNS/DHCP packet processing. The asynchronous queue architecture prevents this deadlock scenario.

```mermaid
graph TB
subgraph "Dnsmasq Event Loop Thread"
    DNS[DNS Query Handler] -->|Log Event| Queue[Non-Blocking Log Queue]
    DHCP[DHCP Server] -->|Log Event| Queue
    Error[Error Conditions] -->|Log Event| Queue
    
    Queue -->|Append to Queue| MemQueue[In-Memory FIFO<br/>Linked List]
end

subgraph "Asynchronous Write Path"
    MemQueue -->|POLLOUT Event| Writer[Non-Blocking Socket Write]
    Writer -->|EAGAIN?| Retry[Return to Event Loop]
    Writer -->|Success?| NextMsg[Dequeue Next Message]
    
    Retry -.->|Socket Writable| Writer
    NextMsg --> Writer
end

subgraph "Syslog Daemon"
    UnixSocket["/dev/log<br/>Unix Domain Socket"] --> Syslog["syslogd/rsyslog"]
    Syslog --> File["/var/log/syslog"]
    Syslog --> Remote[Remote Syslog Servers]
end

Writer -->|Write| UnixSocket

style Queue fill:#fff4e1,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px
style Writer fill:#e1f5ff,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px
style MemQueue fill:#ffe1e1,stroke:#333
```

**Queue Parameters**:

| Parameter | Default Value | Configuration | Purpose |
|-----------|--------------|---------------|---------|
| **Queue Depth** | 5 messages | `--log-async=N` | Maximum pending messages before overflow |
| **Message Size** | 1024 bytes | MAX_MESSAGE constant (RFC 3164) | Maximum single log message length |
| **Overflow Behavior** | Discard oldest | Hardcoded | Prevents memory exhaustion |
| **Overflow Reporting** | After drain | Automatic | Log `overflow: N log entries lost` |

**Queue Implementation** (`src/log.c` lines 47-52):

```c
struct log_entry {
    int offset;                    // Current write position in buffer
    int length;                    // Total message length
    pid_t pid;                     // Process ID (detect fork)
    char payload[MAX_MESSAGE];     // Message buffer (1024 bytes)
    struct log_entry *next;        // Linked list pointer
};
```

**Write Mechanism** (`src/log.c` lines 164-284):

1. **Attempt immediate write** via `log_write()` to `/dev/log` Unix socket
2. **Socket set to O_NONBLOCK**: Never blocks main event loop
3. **EAGAIN/EWOULDBLOCK handling**: Returns control to event loop, retries when socket becomes writable
4. **Event loop integration**: `set_log_writer()` registers socket with `poll()` for POLLOUT events
5. **Overflow protection**: If queue fills before drain, oldest message is discarded

**Benefit**: DNS queries receive <1ms response times even when syslog is slow, ensuring monitoring overhead never degrades service quality.

##### 6.5.2.3.2 Log Destinations

**Syslog (Default)**:

```bash
# /etc/dnsmasq.conf
log-facility=local0  # Custom syslog facility
```

- **Socket Path**: `/dev/log` (Linux) or `/var/run/log` (BSD)
- **Transport**: SOCK_DGRAM (preferred) or SOCK_STREAM (fallback)
- **Format**: RFC 3164 syslog protocol with priority and timestamp
- **Facility**: LOG_DAEMON (default), configurable via `--log-facility`

**File Logging**:

```bash
# /etc/dnsmasq.conf
log-file=/var/log/dnsmasq-custom.log
log-async=50  # Increase queue depth for high-volume logging
```

- **Direct Write**: Bypasses syslog, writes directly to specified file
- **Format**: Timestamped plain text (not syslog format)
- **Rotation Support**: Send SIGUSR2 to reopen log file (enables logrotate integration)

**Stderr (Debug Mode)**:

```bash
dnsmasq --no-daemon --log-file=-
```

- **Use Case**: Foreground debugging and development
- **Format**: Plain text without syslog headers
- **Synchronous**: No queue, immediate writes

**Android Logging** (Conditional: __ANDROID__):

- **Implementation**: `__android_log_vprint()` Android logging API
- **Priority Mapping**: LOG_ERR→ANDROID_LOG_ERROR, LOG_WARNING→ANDROID_LOG_WARN, etc.
- **Destination**: Android logcat system

##### 6.5.2.3.3 Logging Verbosity Levels

**Default (Minimal Logging)**:

- Startup/shutdown messages (LOG_INFO)
- Errors (LOG_ERR): Configuration errors, socket failures, upstream timeouts
- Warnings (LOG_WARNING): Non-critical issues, deprecated options, capacity warnings
- Critical events (LOG_CRIT): Fatal errors requiring process termination

**`--log-queries` (Verbose DNS Query Logging)**:

Logs every DNS transaction with full details:

```
Nov  5 10:35:22 router dnsmasq[1234]: query[A] example.com from 192.168.1.10
Nov  5 10:35:22 router dnsmasq[1234]: forwarded example.com to 8.8.8.8
Nov  5 10:35:22 router dnsmasq[1234]: reply example.com is 93.184.216.34
```

**Performance Impact**: Can generate **hundreds of lines per second** on busy networks. Increase `--log-async` queue depth to 50-100 to prevent overflow.

**`--log-dhcp` (Verbose DHCP Transaction Logging)**:

Logs all DHCP protocol exchanges:

```
Nov  5 10:40:15 router dnsmasq-dhcp[1234]: DHCPDISCOVER(eth0) aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff
Nov  5 10:40:15 router dnsmasq-dhcp[1234]: DHCPOFFER(eth0) 192.168.1.100 aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff
Nov  5 10:40:15 router dnsmasq-dhcp[1234]: DHCPREQUEST(eth0) 192.168.1.100 aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff
Nov  5 10:40:15 router dnsmasq-dhcp[1234]: DHCPACK(eth0) 192.168.1.100 aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff laptop01
```

**`--log-debug` (Debug Logging)**:

Enables extensive debugging output including internal state changes, cache operations, packet parsing details. **Not recommended for production** due to extreme volume.

##### 6.5.2.3.4 Logging Facilities (Message Tags)

**Purpose**: Separate log streams for different subsystems to enable syslog filtering and routing

| Facility Tag | Log Message Prefix | Subsystem | Configuration |
|-------------|-------------------|-----------|---------------|
| Default | `dnsmasq[PID]` | Core DNS operations | Always enabled |
| MS_DHCP | `dnsmasq-dhcp[PID]` | DHCP subsystem | Enabled with `--log-dhcp` |
| MS_TFTP | `dnsmasq-tftp[PID]` | TFTP subsystem | Automatic |
| MS_SCRIPT | `dnsmasq-script[PID]` | Script execution | Automatic |
| MS_DEBUG | No prefix change | Debug messages | Enabled with `--log-debug` |

**Syslog Filtering Example** (`/etc/rsyslog.d/dnsmasq.conf`):

```bash
# Route DHCP logs to separate file
:programname, isequal, "dnsmasq-dhcp" /var/log/dnsmasq-dhcp.log
& stop

#### Route DNS queries to high-speed storage
:programname, isequal, "dnsmasq" /var/log/dnsmasq-dns.log

#### Forward all dnsmasq logs to remote syslog server for aggregation
:programname, startswith, "dnsmasq" @@siem.company.com:514
```

#### 6.5.2.4 Packet Capture for Deep Troubleshooting

**Implementation**: `src/dump.c` (optional: HAVE_DUMPFILE)

**Purpose**: Low-level packet capture in PCAP format for protocol analysis

**Configuration**:

```bash
dnsmasq --dump-file=/var/log/dnsmasq.pcap --dump-mask=0xFFFF
```

**Supported Packet Types**:

- DNS (UDP and TCP)
- DHCPv4 and DHCPv6
- ICMPv6 (Router Advertisement, Neighbor Discovery)
- TFTP

**Features**:

- **PCAP Format**: Compatible with Wireshark, tcpdump, tshark
- **Append Mode**: Can resume packet capture to existing file
- **Named Pipe Support**: Real-time analysis with Wireshark

**Real-Time Wireshark Analysis**:

```bash
# Create named pipe
mkfifo /tmp/dnsmasq.pcap

#### Start Wireshark in capture mode
wireshark -k -i /tmp/dnsmasq.pcap &

#### Start dnsmasq with packet dumping
dnsmasq --dump-file=/tmp/dnsmasq.pcap
```

**Use Cases**:

- **DNSSEC Validation Failures**: Inspect RRSIG records, DS lookups, trust chain
- **Malformed DHCP Packets**: Analyze vendor-specific options, relay agent information
- **Protocol Implementation Issues**: Verify RFC compliance, troubleshoot interoperability
- **Security Analysis**: Capture evidence of DNS poisoning attempts, DHCP spoofing

#### 6.5.2.5 Distributed Tracing: Not Applicable

**Architectural Limitation**: Dnsmasq's single-threaded, event-driven architecture does not support distributed tracing instrumentation (OpenTelemetry, Jaeger, Zipkin).

**Query Correlation**: DNS queries have a `log_id` field (`src/dnsmasq.h` line 1292) for local log correlation within a single process, but this is **not a distributed trace ID**. The query ID enables linking log entries for a single query's lifecycle (reception → cache miss → upstream forward → response → cache population → client reply) but does not propagate across systems.

**Implication**: Cannot trace a DNS query through multiple systems (client → dnsmasq → upstream DNS → authoritative server) with trace IDs. External distributed tracing requires instrumentation at the network level (eBPF, packet capture analysis) rather than application-level tracing.

### 6.5.3 Observability Patterns

#### 6.5.3.1 Health Check Mechanisms

**No Built-In Health Check Endpoint**: Dnsmasq does not provide HTTP/REST health check endpoints (e.g., `/health`, `/ready`, `/live`) common in modern microservices.

##### 6.5.3.1.1 Systemd Integration Health Checks

**Service Type**: `Type=dbus` (`contrib/systemd/dnsmasq.service` line 7)

Systemd monitors D-Bus service registration as health indicator:

```ini
[Service]
Type=dbus
BusName=uk.org.thekelleys.dnsmasq
ExecStartPre=/usr/sbin/dnsmasq --test
ExecStart=/usr/sbin/dnsmasq -k
Restart=always
RestartSec=5s
```

**Pre-Start Validation**:

```bash
/usr/sbin/dnsmasq --test
```

- Validates configuration syntax before starting service
- Returns non-zero exit code if configuration invalid
- Catches syntax errors, invalid addresses, missing files
- Prevents bad configuration from disrupting running service

**Service Monitoring**:

- Systemd waits for D-Bus service `uk.org.thekelleys.dnsmasq` to appear on system bus
- Automatic restart on process crash
- Startup timeout detection (default 90 seconds)
- Logs to journald: `journalctl -u dnsmasq -f`

##### 6.5.3.1.2 Process-Based Health Checks

**PID File Check**:

```bash
#!/bin/bash
# Basic health check script
PID_FILE="/var/run/dnsmasq.pid"

if [ -f "$PID_FILE" ]; then
    PID=$(cat "$PID_FILE")
    if kill -0 "$PID" 2>/dev/null; then
        echo "dnsmasq is running (PID: $PID)"
        exit 0
    fi
fi

echo "dnsmasq is not running"
exit 1
```

**D-Bus Health Check** (requires D-Bus enabled):

```bash
#!/bin/bash
# Query dnsmasq via D-Bus to verify service responsiveness
timeout 5 dbus-send --system --print-reply \
    --dest=uk.org.thekelleys.dnsmasq \
    /uk/org/thekelleys/dnsmasq \
    uk.org.thekelleys.dnsmasq.GetVersion >/dev/null 2>&1

if [ $? -eq 0 ]; then
    echo "dnsmasq is responsive"
    exit 0
else
    echo "dnsmasq is unresponsive or not running"
    exit 1
fi
```

##### 6.5.3.1.3 Functional Health Checks

**DNS Health Check**:

```bash
#!/bin/bash
# Query local dnsmasq for test domain
RESULT=$(dig @127.0.0.1 +short +timeout=2 google.com A 2>/dev/null)

if [ -n "$RESULT" ]; then
    echo "DNS service is functional"
    exit 0
else
    echo "DNS service failed to resolve query"
    exit 1
fi
```

**DHCP Health Check**:

```bash
#!/bin/bash
# Verify lease file is recent (updated within last hour)
LEASE_FILE="/var/lib/misc/dnsmasq.leases"

if [ -f "$LEASE_FILE" ]; then
    AGE=$(( $(date +%s) - $(stat -c %Y "$LEASE_FILE") ))
    if [ $AGE -lt 3600 ]; then
        echo "DHCP service is active (lease file updated ${AGE}s ago)"
        exit 0
    fi
fi

echo "DHCP service may be inactive (lease file stale or missing)"
exit 1
```

#### 6.5.3.2 Performance Metrics and Calculation

##### 6.5.3.2.1 DNS Performance Indicators

**Cache Hit Ratio**:

```
cache_hit_ratio = dns_local_answered / (dns_local_answered + dns_queries_forwarded)

Target: 70-90% for typical small network workloads
```

**Cache Efficiency (LRU Pressure)**:

```
lru_efficiency = 1.0 - (dns_cache_live_freed / dns_cache_inserted)

<0.9 (>10% evictions): Cache too small, consider increasing --cache-size
>0.95 (<5% evictions): Cache adequately sized
```

**Upstream Error Rate**:

```
error_rate = dns_unanswered_query / (dns_queries_forwarded + dns_local_answered)

<1%: Normal operation
1-5%: Degraded upstream connectivity
>5%: Critical upstream failure
```

**Stale Cache Serving (Upstream Availability)**:

```
upstream_availability = 1.0 - (dns_stale_answered / dns_queries_forwarded)

=1.0: All upstreams healthy
<0.95: Partial upstream failure
<0.90: Multiple upstream failures, degraded service
```

##### 6.5.3.2.2 DHCP Performance Indicators

**Pool Exhaustion Detection**:

```
exhaustion_events = METRIC_NOANSWER

>0: Address pool exhaustion occurred (CRITICAL ALERT)
=0: Adequate address pool capacity
```

**Lease Churn Rate**:

```
churn_rate = (leases_allocated - leases_pruned) / time_interval

Stable network: Low churn (few allocations/expirations per hour)
Transient clients: High churn (many allocations/expirations per minute)
```

**DHCP DECLINE Rate (IP Conflict Indicator)**:

```
conflict_rate = dhcp_decline / dhcp_ack

<0.01 (<1%): Normal operation
>0.05 (>5%): Significant IP conflicts, investigate rogue DHCP servers or static IP collisions
```

##### 6.5.3.2.3 Upstream Server Performance

**Per-Server Query Success Rate**:

```
success_rate = (queries - failed_queries) / queries

>0.95: Healthy server
0.90-0.95: Degraded performance
<0.90: Failing server, should be removed or investigated
```

**Per-Server Average Latency**:

Calculated by dnsmasq internally:

```
average_latency_ms = query_latency / (queries - failed_queries)

<50ms: Excellent
50-100ms: Good
100-200ms: Acceptable
>200ms: Poor, consider alternative upstream
```

**Note**: Dnsmasq does NOT track latency percentiles (p50, p95, p99). Only average latency is available. External monitoring systems must collect samples and compute percentiles if required.

#### 6.5.3.3 Business Metrics: Not Applicable

Dnsmasq does **not track business-level metrics** such as:

- ❌ Revenue, transactions, or user sessions
- ❌ Customer engagement or conversion rates
- ❌ Service tier utilization or licensing compliance
- ❌ Geographic distribution of requests

The system provides only **technical operational metrics** (queries, leases, errors). Closest equivalents to business metrics:

- **Service Utilization**: Total queries processed (`dns_queries_forwarded + dns_local_answered`)
- **Service Quality**: Error rates, DHCP DECLINE rates
- **Capacity Utilization**: Lease allocation rates, cache insertion rates

#### 6.5.3.4 SLA Monitoring and Compliance

##### 6.5.3.4.1 Documented SLA Targets

From Technical Specification Section 4.10.1 Performance Characteristics:

| Operation | Target Latency | SLA Target | Measurement Method |
|-----------|---------------|------------|-------------------|
| **DNS Cache Hit** | <1ms | 99.9% achieve target | External timing measurement |
| **DNS Cache Miss (UDP)** | Upstream + 5-10ms | 95% <100ms total | External timing measurement |
| **DNS over TCP** | Upstream + 10-20ms | 90% <200ms total | External timing measurement |
| **DNSSEC Validation** | Upstream + 20-100ms | 90% <500ms total | External timing measurement |
| **DHCPv4 DISCOVER→ACK** | 5-20ms | 99% <50ms | External timing measurement |
| **DHCPv6 SOLICIT→REPLY** | 5-20ms | 99% <50ms | External timing measurement |
| **DHCP Lease Renewal** | 5-10ms | 99.9% <20ms | External timing measurement |
| **Configuration Reload** | 100-500ms | 99% <1s | SIGHUP timestamp to service resumed |

##### 6.5.3.4.2 SLA Enforcement Strategy

**No Automated SLA Tracking**: Dnsmasq does not:

- ❌ Measure response time percentiles internally
- ❌ Calculate uptime percentages
- ❌ Track SLA compliance automatically
- ❌ Generate SLA violation alerts

**External Monitoring Required**:

SLA compliance must be measured by external monitoring systems:

1. **Active Probing**: Send test DNS queries at regular intervals, measure response times
2. **Metrics Polling**: Query D-Bus/UBus metrics every 30-60 seconds
3. **Derived Metrics Calculation**: Compute cache hit ratios, error rates, latency estimates
4. **Threshold Comparison**: Compare against SLA targets
5. **Alert Generation**: Trigger alerts when thresholds exceeded

**Example Prometheus Alert Rules**:

```yaml
groups:
  - name: dnsmasq_sla
    rules:
      - alert: DnsmasqHighQueryLatency
        expr: avg_over_time(dnsmasq_server_avg_latency_ms[5m]) > 100
        for: 5m
        labels:
          severity: warning
        annotations:
          summary: "Dnsmasq upstream latency exceeding SLA"
          description: "Average upstream latency {{ $value }}ms (target <50ms)"
      
      - alert: DnsmasqLowCacheHitRatio
        expr: |
          (dnsmasq_dns_local_answered / 
           (dnsmasq_dns_local_answered + dnsmasq_dns_queries_forwarded)) < 0.70
        for: 10m
        labels:
          severity: warning
        annotations:
          summary: "Dnsmasq cache hit ratio below target"
          description: "Cache hit ratio {{ $value }} (target >70%)"
      
      - alert: DnsmasqDHCPPoolExhaustion
        expr: increase(dnsmasq_noanswer_total[5m]) > 0
        labels:
          severity: critical
        annotations:
          summary: "DHCP address pool exhausted"
          description: "{{ $value }} NOANSWER events in last 5 minutes"
```

#### 6.5.3.5 Capacity Tracking

##### 6.5.3.5.1 DNS Cache Capacity

**Metric Limitation**: Dnsmasq does **not track current cache fill level** (number of entries currently stored). Only cache insertions and evictions are counted.

**Inference Method**:

1. Trigger SIGUSR1 cache dump with `--log-queries` enabled
2. Parse syslog output to count cache entries
3. Compare against configured `--cache-size` value

**LRU Eviction Indicator**:

```
cache_pressure = dns_cache_live_freed / dns_cache_inserted

<0.05: Cache lightly utilized
0.05-0.10: Moderate cache pressure
>0.10: High cache pressure, consider increasing --cache-size
```

**Recommendation**: If `dns_cache_live_freed` consistently >10% of `dns_cache_inserted`, increase cache size by 2-5x to reduce upstream query load.

##### 6.5.3.5.2 DHCP Address Pool Capacity

**Metric Limitation**: Dnsmasq does **not track available addresses in pool**. Only allocation and pruning events are counted.

**Inference Method**:

```bash
# Count active leases
ACTIVE_LEASES=$(wc -l < /var/lib/misc/dnsmasq.leases)

#### Compare against configured pool size
#### Example: dhcp-range=192.168.1.100,192.168.1.200 (101 addresses)
POOL_SIZE=101
UTILIZATION=$(echo "scale=2; $ACTIVE_LEASES / $POOL_SIZE" | bc)

echo "DHCP pool utilization: ${UTILIZATION}%"
```

**Exhaustion Detection**:

```
pool_exhausted = (METRIC_NOANSWER > 0)

If true: CRITICAL - expand address range or reduce lease time
```

##### 6.5.3.5.3 TCP Connection Capacity

**Current Connections**: `METRIC_TCP_CONNECTIONS` (real-time value)

**Peak Connections**: Tracked in `daemon->max_procs_used` (`src/cache.c` lines 2084-2088), reported in SIGUSR1 dump

**Capacity Planning**:

```
connection_utilization = current_tcp_connections / MAX_PROCS

MAX_PROCS = 20 (default, recompile to change)

<0.50: Adequate capacity
0.50-0.80: Moderate load
>0.80: High load, consider increasing MAX_PROCS or investigating slow clients
```

**Typical Scenarios Causing High TCP Connection Count**:

- DNS over TCP for large responses (DNSSEC records)
- Misbehaving clients not closing TCP connections
- Slow network links preventing timely connection closure

##### 6.5.3.5.4 File Descriptor Capacity

**Not Tracked Internally**: Dnsmasq does not monitor its own file descriptor usage.

**External Monitoring**:

```bash
# Check current FD usage
PID=$(cat /var/run/dnsmasq.pid)
FD_COUNT=$(ls /proc/$PID/fd | wc -l)
FD_LIMIT=$(ulimit -n)

echo "File descriptors: $FD_COUNT / $FD_LIMIT"

#### List open file descriptors
lsof -p $PID
```

**Typical FD Consumption**:

- Listening sockets: 2-20 (DNS UDP/TCP, DHCP, TFTP, netlink, D-Bus)
- Active TCP connections: 0-20 (MAX_PROCS limit)
- Log socket: 1 (`/dev/log`)
- Configuration files: Closed after reading
- Lease file: Opened briefly for writes, closed immediately

**Exhaustion Scenario**:

If process hits RLIMIT_NOFILE limit:

- New TCP connections fail with EMFILE error
- UDP continues normally (sockets pre-created)
- Logged: `failed to accept connection: Too many open files`

### 6.5.4 Incident Response Capabilities

#### 6.5.4.1 Alert Routing: External Systems Required

**No Built-In Alerting**: Dnsmasq **never generates alerts**. It logs events; external systems interpret significance and generate alerts.

##### 6.5.4.1.1 Alert Sources (External Integration)

**Syslog Events**:

External syslog monitoring (rsyslog, syslog-ng, Splunk, ELK) can pattern-match critical events:

```bash
# rsyslog configuration for alerting
# /etc/rsyslog.d/dnsmasq-alerts.conf

#### DHCP pool exhaustion (CRITICAL)
:programname, isequal, "dnsmasq-dhcp" :msg, contains, "no address available" \
    ^/usr/local/bin/alert-dhcp-exhaustion.sh

#### Configuration reload failure (WARNING)
:programname, isequal, "dnsmasq" :msg, contains, "Failed to reload" \
    /var/log/dnsmasq-alerts.log

#### Upstream DNS server failure (WARNING)
:programname, isequal, "dnsmasq" :msg, regex, "server .* failed" \
    /var/log/dnsmasq-alerts.log
```

**Metrics Thresholds**:

External monitoring polls D-Bus/UBus metrics and evaluates thresholds:

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
# External monitoring script (cron: */5 * * * *)

import dbus
import sys

bus = dbus.SystemBus()
dnsmasq = dbus.Interface(
    bus.get_object('uk.org.thekelleys.dnsmasq', '/uk/org/thekelleys/dnsmasq'),
    'uk.org.thekelleys.dnsmasq'
)

metrics = dnsmasq.GetMetrics()

#### Alert on pool exhaustion
if metrics['noanswer'] > 0:
    print("CRITICAL: DHCP pool exhausted", file=sys.stderr)
#### Send alert via PagerDuty, email, webhook, etc.
    send_alert(severity='critical', message='DHCP pool exhaustion detected')

#### Alert on high error rate
total_queries = metrics['dns_local_answered'] + metrics['dns_queries_forwarded']
error_rate = metrics['dns_unanswered_query'] / total_queries if total_queries > 0 else 0

if error_rate > 0.05:
    print(f"WARNING: High DNS error rate {error_rate:.2%}", file=sys.stderr)
    send_alert(severity='warning', message=f'DNS error rate {error_rate:.2%}')
```

**Process Health**:

Systemd failure alerts:

```bash
# /etc/systemd/system/dnsmasq-alert.service
[Unit]
Description=Dnsmasq Failure Alert
After=dnsmasq.service
BindsTo=dnsmasq.service

[Service]
Type=oneshot
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/send-alert.sh "Dnsmasq failed to start"
```

```bash
# /usr/local/bin/send-alert.sh
#!/bin/bash
MESSAGE="$1"
# Send to monitoring system (PagerDuty, Opsgenie, Slack, email)
curl -X POST https://monitoring.company.com/api/alerts \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d "{\"service\": \"dnsmasq\", \"severity\": \"critical\", \"message\": \"$MESSAGE\"}"
```

##### 6.5.4.1.2 Example Alert Patterns

**Critical Alerts**:

| Condition | Detection Method | Severity | Response Time SLA |
|-----------|-----------------|----------|------------------|
| Process crash | systemd monitoring | Critical | Immediate (auto-restart) |
| DHCP pool exhaustion | `METRIC_NOANSWER > 0` | Critical | 15 minutes |
| All upstreams failed | syslog pattern match | Critical | 15 minutes |
| Configuration reload failure | syslog pattern match | Critical | 30 minutes |

**Warning Alerts**:

| Condition | Detection Method | Severity | Response Time SLA |
|-----------|-----------------|----------|------------------|
| High DNS error rate | `error_rate > 5%` | Warning | 1 hour |
| Low cache hit ratio | `cache_hit_ratio < 0.70` | Warning | 4 hours |
| Single upstream failure | per-server metrics | Warning | 1 hour |
| High cache eviction rate | `lru_efficiency < 0.90` | Warning | 4 hours |

#### 6.5.4.2 Escalation Procedures: External Implementation

**No Built-In Escalation**: Dnsmasq has no concept of:

- ❌ Escalation policies
- ❌ On-call schedules
- ❌ Paging integration
- ❌ Alert deduplication
- ❌ Time-based escalation rules

**External Escalation Implementation** (PagerDuty/Opsgenie example):

```yaml
# PagerDuty escalation policy
escalation_policies:
  - name: dnsmasq-critical
    escalation_rules:
      - escalation_delay_in_minutes: 0
        targets:
          - type: user
            id: oncall-primary
      
      - escalation_delay_in_minutes: 15
        targets:
          - type: user
            id: oncall-secondary
      
      - escalation_delay_in_minutes: 30
        targets:
          - type: schedule
            id: engineering-manager

services:
  - name: dnsmasq
    escalation_policy: dnsmasq-critical
    alert_grouping: time
    alert_grouping_timeout: 300
```

#### 6.5.4.3 Runbooks and Remediation

**No Automated Runbook Execution**: Dnsmasq does not execute runbooks or remediation scripts automatically in response to problems.

##### 6.5.4.3.1 Example Runbooks (Operator-Executed)

**Runbook 1: DHCP Address Pool Exhaustion**

```
## Symptoms
- Clients cannot obtain IP addresses
- Syslog contains: "no address available for <MAC>"
- METRIC_NOANSWER > 0

#### Investigation Steps
1. Check active lease count:
   ```bash
   wc -l /var/lib/misc/dnsmasq.leases
   ```

2. Verify configured address range:
   ```bash
   grep "^dhcp-range" /etc/dnsmasq.conf
   ```

3. Check for expired leases not being pruned:
   ```bash
   awk '{print $1, $3}' /var/lib/misc/dnsmasq.leases | \
   while read expire ip; do
       if [ $expire -lt $(date +%s) ]; then
           echo "Expired lease: $ip (expired $(date -d @$expire))"
       fi
   done
   ```

#### Resolution Options

**Option A: Expand Address Range** (if IP space available):
```bash
# Edit /etc/dnsmasq.conf
# Change: dhcp-range=192.168.1.100,192.168.1.200,24h
# To:     dhcp-range=192.168.1.50,192.168.1.250,24h

#### Reload configuration
systemctl reload dnsmasq

#### Verify expansion
kill -USR1 $(cat /var/run/dnsmasq.pid)
grep "DHCP, IP range" /var/log/syslog
```

**Option B: Reduce Lease Time** (increase churn):
```bash
# Edit /etc/dnsmasq.conf
# Change: dhcp-range=192.168.1.100,192.168.1.200,24h
# To:     dhcp-range=192.168.1.100,192.168.1.200,4h

#### Reload configuration
systemctl reload dnsmasq
```

**Option C: Manual Lease Cleanup** (emergency):
```bash
# Stop dnsmasq
systemctl stop dnsmasq

#### Backup lease file
cp /var/lib/misc/dnsmasq.leases /var/lib/misc/dnsmasq.leases.backup

#### Remove expired leases manually
NOW=$(date +%s)
awk -v now=$NOW '$1 > now' /var/lib/misc/dnsmasq.leases.backup \
    > /var/lib/misc/dnsmasq.leases

#### Restart dnsmasq
systemctl start dnsmasq
```

#### Prevention
- Monitor `METRIC_NOANSWER` metric; alert if >0
- Set up capacity alerting at 80% pool utilization
- Implement automatic lease time adjustment based on pool usage
```

**Runbook 2: All Upstream DNS Servers Failed**

```
## Symptoms
- DNS queries fail with SERVFAIL
- Syslog contains: "no servers found in /etc/resolv.conf"
- High `dns_unanswered_query` metric
- Stale cache serving enabled: `dns_stale_answered` increasing

#### Investigation Steps
1. Check dnsmasq cache dump:
   ```bash
   kill -USR1 $(cat /var/run/dnsmasq.pid)
   grep "server.*failed" /var/log/syslog | tail -20
   ```

2. Verify upstream server connectivity:
   ```bash
   for server in 8.8.8.8 1.1.1.1 208.67.222.222; do
       echo -n "Testing $server: "
       dig @$server +timeout=5 google.com +short || echo "FAILED"
   done
   ```

3. Check network routing:
   ```bash
   traceroute 8.8.8.8
   ```

#### Resolution Options

**Option A: Add Working Upstream Servers**:
```bash
# Test alternative upstream servers
dig @1.1.1.1 +timeout=5 google.com  # Cloudflare
dig @9.9.9.9 +timeout=5 google.com  # Quad9

#### Add to /etc/dnsmasq.conf
echo "server=1.1.1.1" >> /etc/dnsmasq.conf
echo "server=1.0.0.1" >> /etc/dnsmasq.conf

#### Reload
systemctl reload dnsmasq
```

**Option B: Investigate Network Outage**:
```bash
# Check firewall rules blocking DNS
iptables -L OUTPUT -n -v | grep 53

#### Check if network interface is up
ip link show

#### Check default route
ip route show

#### Test ICMP connectivity
ping -c 5 8.8.8.8
```

**Option C: Temporary Local Resolution** (emergency):
```bash
# Add emergency entries to /etc/hosts for critical domains
echo "93.184.216.34 example.com" >> /etc/hosts

#### Reload dnsmasq (reads /etc/hosts)
systemctl reload dnsmasq
```

#### Prevention
- Configure geographically diverse upstream servers
- Monitor per-server failure rates; alert if any server >10% failures
- Implement automated upstream server health checks
- Configure `--cache-max-expiry=86400` to serve stale cache longer during outages
```

**Runbook 3: High DNS Query Latency**

```
## Symptoms
- Client-reported slow DNS resolution
- Average upstream latency >100ms (from SIGUSR1 dump)
- Performance SLA violations

#### Investigation Steps
1. Check per-server latency:
   ```bash
   kill -USR1 $(cat /var/run/dnsmasq.pid)
   grep "server.*avg. latency" /var/log/syslog | tail -20
   ```

2. Test upstream servers directly:
   ```bash
   for server in 8.8.8.8 1.1.1.1; do
       echo "Testing $server:"
       time dig @$server +timeout=5 google.com
   done
   ```

3. Check cache hit ratio:
   ```bash
   # Poll D-Bus metrics
   python3 -c "
   import dbus
   bus = dbus.SystemBus()
   m = dbus.Interface(
       bus.get_object('uk.org.thekelleys.dnsmasq', '/uk/org/thekelleys/dnsmasq'),
       'uk.org.thekelleys.dnsmasq'
   ).GetMetrics()
   
   total = m['dns_local_answered'] + m['dns_queries_forwarded']
   hit_ratio = m['dns_local_answered'] / total if total > 0 else 0
   print(f'Cache hit ratio: {hit_ratio:.2%}')
   print(f'Cache insertions: {m[\"dns_cache_inserted\"]}')
   print(f'Cache evictions: {m[\"dns_cache_live_freed\"]}')
   "
   ```

#### Resolution Options

**Option A: Replace Slow Upstream Servers**:
```bash
# Remove slow server from /etc/dnsmasq.conf
# (edit file, remove "server=<slow_server>" line)

#### Add faster alternatives
echo "server=1.1.1.1" >> /etc/dnsmasq.conf  # Cloudflare (typically fast)
echo "server=8.8.8.8" >> /etc/dnsmasq.conf  # Google (typically fast)

#### Reload
systemctl reload dnsmasq
```

**Option B: Increase Cache Size** (reduce upstream queries):
```bash
# Edit /etc/dnsmasq.conf
echo "cache-size=5000" >> /etc/dnsmasq.conf

#### Reload
systemctl reload dnsmasq
```

**Option C: Investigate Network Path**:
```bash
# MTR to upstream servers (identifies network problems)
mtr -r -c 100 8.8.8.8

#### Check for packet loss
ping -c 100 8.8.8.8 | grep loss
```

#### Prevention
- Monitor average latency per upstream server; alert if >100ms
- Periodically benchmark upstream servers and rotate to fastest options
- Increase cache size proactively before hit ratio degrades
- Configure geographically nearby upstream servers
```

#### 6.5.4.4 Post-Mortem Processes

**No Built-In Post-Mortem Tools**: Dnsmasq does not capture:

- ❌ Incident timelines
- ❌ Root cause analysis templates
- ❌ Blameless post-mortem structures
- ❌ Automated incident reports

##### 6.5.4.4.1 Post-Mortem Data Sources

**Syslog History**:

```bash
# Extract relevant time window (example: Nov 5 10:00-11:00)
journalctl -u dnsmasq \
    --since "2025-11-05 10:00:00" \
    --until "2025-11-05 11:00:00" \
    > incident-2025-11-05-dnsmasq.log

#### Search for errors during incident
grep -i "error\|fail\|critical" incident-2025-11-05-dnsmasq.log
```

**Cache Dumps**:

```bash
# If SIGUSR1 was triggered during incident, cache state is logged
grep "^Nov  5 10:" /var/log/syslog | grep "dnsmasq\[.*\]: cache size"
```

**Packet Captures** (if enabled):

```bash
# Analyze PCAP captured during incident
wireshark dnsmasq-incident-2025-11-05.pcap

#### Extract statistics
tshark -r dnsmasq-incident-2025-11-05.pcap -q -z io,stat,60
```

**Configuration History**:

```bash
# Review configuration changes (requires version control)
git log --since="2025-11-01" --until="2025-11-06" -- /etc/dnsmasq.conf
git diff HEAD~5:etc/dnsmasq.conf HEAD:etc/dnsmasq.conf
```

##### 6.5.4.4.2 Post-Mortem Template (Manual)

```

- **HH:MM** - Service restored: [Verification method]
- **HH:MM** - Incident closed: [Final status]

[Detailed description of the incident, technical explanation]

#### Why It Happened
[Underlying cause: configuration error, capacity limit, upstream failure, etc.]

#### Evidence

```
[Paste relevant log entries]
```

#### Metrics at Time of Incident
```
DNS Cache Hit Ratio: X%
Upstream Server Latency: Xms
DHCP Pool Utilization: X%
METRIC_NOANSWER: X
```

[Relevant configuration excerpts]
```

#### 6.5.4.5 Improvement Tracking

**No Built-In Issue Tracking**: Dnsmasq does not:

- ❌ Track issues, feature requests, or improvements internally
- ❌ Maintain backlog of operational improvements
- ❌ Provide project management or kanban boards

**External Improvement Process**:

1. **Issue Reporting**: GitHub issues, mailing list (dnsmasq-discuss@lists.thekelleys.org.uk)
2. **Configuration Management**: Version control for config files (Git, Ansible, Puppet, Chef)
3. **Change Management**: Review/approval process for configuration changes
4. **Deployment Tracking**: Infrastructure-as-code logs (Ansible playbook runs, Chef client logs)

**Example Configuration Change Workflow**:

```bash
# 1. Create feature branch
git checkout -b increase-dhcp-pool

#### Make configuration change
sed -i 's/dhcp-range=192.168.1.100,192.168.1.200/dhcp-range=192.168.1.50,192.168.1.250/' \
    /etc/dnsmasq.conf

#### Test configuration
dnsmasq --test --conf-file=/etc/dnsmasq.conf

#### Commit and push for review
git add /etc/dnsmasq.conf
git commit -m "Expand DHCP pool to 201 addresses to address exhaustion alerts"
git push origin increase-dhcp-pool

#### Create pull request for peer review

#### After approval, deploy via configuration management
ansible-playbook deploy-dnsmasq-config.yml

#### Verify deployment
systemctl reload dnsmasq
kill -USR1 $(cat /var/run/dnsmasq.pid)
grep "DHCP, IP range" /var/log/syslog

#### Track deployment in change log
echo "$(date): Deployed DHCP pool expansion (Ticket OPS-1234)" >> /var/log/changes.log
```

**Example Grafana Dashboard Panels**:

| Panel Title | Query | Visualization | Alert Threshold |
|-------------|-------|---------------|----------------|
| **Cache Hit Ratio** | `dnsmasq_dns_local_answered / (dnsmasq_dns_local_answered + dnsmasq_dns_queries_forwarded)` | Time series graph | <0.70 (warning) |
| **Queries per Second** | `rate(dnsmasq_dns_local_answered[5m]) + rate(dnsmasq_dns_queries_forwarded[5m])` | Graph with gradient | >10,000 (capacity warning) |
| **DHCP Pool Utilization** | `count(active_leases) / dhcp_pool_size` | Gauge (0-100%) | >80% (warning), >95% (critical) |
| **Upstream Avg Latency** | `dnsmasq_server_avg_latency_ms` | Multi-series graph | >100ms (warning) |
| **Error Rate** | `rate(dnsmasq_dns_unanswered_query[5m]) / rate(total_queries[5m])` | Single stat with thresholds | >1% (warning), >5% (critical) |

### 6.5.6 Operational Monitoring Workflows

#### 6.5.6.1 Daily Monitoring Routine

**Automated Checks** (cron or monitoring system):

```bash
#!/bin/bash
# /usr/local/bin/dnsmasq-daily-check.sh
# Run via cron: 0 9 * * * /usr/local/bin/dnsmasq-daily-check.sh

REPORT_FILE="/var/log/dnsmasq-daily-$(date +%Y%m%d).txt"

{
    echo "===== Dnsmasq Daily Health Report ====="
    echo "Date: $(date)"
    echo ""
    
    # 1. Process Health
    echo "=== Process Health ==="
    if systemctl is-active --quiet dnsmasq; then
        echo "✓ Service is active"
        PID=$(cat /var/run/dnsmasq.pid 2>/dev/null)
        echo "  PID: $PID"
        echo "  Uptime: $(ps -p $PID -o etime= 2>/dev/null)"
    else
        echo "✗ Service is NOT active"
    fi
    echo ""
    
    # 2. Trigger cache dump and wait for syslog
    echo "=== Statistics Summary ==="
    kill -USR1 $(cat /var/run/dnsmasq.pid 2>/dev/null)
    sleep 2
    journalctl -u dnsmasq --since "1 minute ago" | \
        grep -E "cache size|queries forwarded|server.*latency"
    echo ""
    
    # 3. Check for errors in last 24 hours
    echo "=== Errors in Last 24 Hours ==="
    ERROR_COUNT=$(journalctl -u dnsmasq --since "24 hours ago" | \
        grep -i "error\|fail\|critical" | wc -l)
    echo "Total errors: $ERROR_COUNT"
    if [ $ERROR_COUNT -gt 0 ]; then
        echo "Recent errors:"
        journalctl -u dnsmasq --since "24 hours ago" | \
            grep -i "error\|fail\|critical" | tail -10
    fi
    echo ""
    
    # 4. DHCP pool status
    echo "=== DHCP Status ==="
    LEASE_COUNT=$(wc -l < /var/lib/misc/dnsmasq.leases 2>/dev/null || echo 0)
    echo "Active leases: $LEASE_COUNT"
    NOANSWER=$(journalctl -u dnsmasq --since "24 hours ago" | \
        grep "no address available" | wc -l)
    if [ $NOANSWER -gt 0 ]; then
        echo "⚠ Pool exhaustion events: $NOANSWER (INVESTIGATE)"
    else
        echo "✓ No pool exhaustion events"
    fi
    echo ""
    
    # 5. Configuration integrity
    echo "=== Configuration Integrity ==="
    if dnsmasq --test 2>&1 | grep -q "syntax check OK"; then
        echo "✓ Configuration syntax valid"
    else
        echo "✗ Configuration syntax INVALID"
        dnsmasq --test 2>&1
    fi
    
} | tee "$REPORT_FILE"

#### Email report to administrators
mail -s "Dnsmasq Daily Health Report - $(hostname)" \
    sysadmin@company.com < "$REPORT_FILE"
```

#### 6.5.6.2 Incident Investigation Workflow

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Alert[Receive Alert<br/>from Monitoring System] --> Type{Alert Type}
    
    Type -->|Process Crash| CheckService[Check systemd status<br/>systemctl status dnsmasq]
    Type -->|High Error Rate| CheckMetrics[Poll D-Bus metrics<br/>dbus-send GetMetrics]
    Type -->|Pool Exhaustion| CheckLeases[Count active leases<br/>wc -l dnsmasq.leases]
    Type -->|High Latency| CheckUpstream[Check upstream servers<br/>dig @<server>]
    
    CheckService --> Logs1[Review recent logs<br/>journalctl -u dnsmasq -n 100]
    CheckMetrics --> Logs1
    CheckLeases --> Logs1
    CheckUpstream --> Logs1
    
    Logs1 --> Pattern{Identify<br/>Pattern}
    
    Pattern -->|Config Error| FixConfig[Edit /etc/dnsmasq.conf<br/>Fix syntax/values]
    Pattern -->|Capacity Limit| Expand[Expand limits<br/>cache-size, dhcp-range]
    Pattern -->|Upstream Failure| SwitchUpstream[Change upstream servers]
    Pattern -->|Unknown| DeepDive[Deep investigation<br/>SIGUSR1 dump, packet capture]
    
    FixConfig --> Test[Test configuration<br/>dnsmasq --test]
    Expand --> Test
    SwitchUpstream --> Test
    
    Test --> Valid{Valid?}
    Valid -->|Yes| Reload[Reload configuration<br/>systemctl reload dnsmasq]
    Valid -->|No| FixConfig
    
    Reload --> Verify[Verify resolution<br/>Check metrics, test queries]
    
    DeepDive --> Capture[Enable packet dump<br/>--dump-file]
    Capture --> Analyze[Analyze with Wireshark<br/>Identify root cause]
    Analyze --> FixConfig
    
    Verify --> Resolved{Resolved?}
    
    Resolved -->|Yes| Document[Document in post-mortem<br/>Update runbook]
    Resolved -->|No| Escalate[Escalate to senior engineer<br/>or vendor support]
    
    Document --> Close[Close incident]
    Escalate --> Close
    
    style Alert fill:#ffe1e1,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px
    style Resolved fill:#e1ffe1,stroke:#333
    style Document fill:#e1f5ff,stroke:#333
```

### 6.5.7 Integration with External Monitoring Systems

#### 6.5.7.1 Prometheus Integration Example

**Step 1: Deploy Prometheus Exporter** (third-party, not in dnsmasq repository)

```bash
# Install dnsmasq_exporter (example: Go-based exporter)
# https://github.com/google/dnsmasq_exporter

#### Run exporter
./dnsmasq_exporter \
    --dnsmasq.address=uk.org.thekelleys.dnsmasq \
    --web.listen-address=:9153

#### Exporter exposes metrics at http://localhost:9153/metrics
```

**Step 2: Configure Prometheus Scraping**

```yaml
# /etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: 'dnsmasq'
    static_configs:
      - targets: ['localhost:9153']
    scrape_interval: 30s
    scrape_timeout: 10s
```

**Step 3: Define Alert Rules**

```yaml
# /etc/prometheus/rules/dnsmasq.yml
groups:
  - name: dnsmasq_alerts
    interval: 30s
    rules:
      - alert: DnsmasqDown
        expr: up{job="dnsmasq"} == 0
        for: 1m
        labels:
          severity: critical
        annotations:
          summary: "Dnsmasq service is down"
          description: "Dnsmasq on {{ $labels.instance }} has been down for more than 1 minute"
      
      - alert: DnsmasqHighErrorRate
        expr: |
          (
            rate(dnsmasq_dns_unanswered_query[5m]) / 
            (rate(dnsmasq_dns_local_answered[5m]) + rate(dnsmasq_dns_queries_forwarded[5m]))
          ) > 0.05
        for: 5m
        labels:
          severity: warning
        annotations:
          summary: "Dnsmasq DNS error rate exceeds 5%"
          description: "Error rate is {{ $value | humanizePercentage }} on {{ $labels.instance }}"
      
      - alert: DnsmasqDHCPPoolExhaustion
        expr: increase(dnsmasq_noanswer_total[5m]) > 0
        labels:
          severity: critical
        annotations:
          summary: "Dnsmasq DHCP pool exhausted"
          description: "{{ $value }} NOANSWER events in last 5 minutes on {{ $labels.instance }}"
      
      - alert: DnsmasqLowCacheHitRatio
        expr: |
          (
            dnsmasq_dns_local_answered / 
            (dnsmasq_dns_local_answered + dnsmasq_dns_queries_forwarded)
          ) < 0.70
        for: 10m
        labels:
          severity: warning
        annotations:
          summary: "Dnsmasq cache hit ratio below 70%"
          description: "Cache hit ratio is {{ $value | humanizePercentage }} on {{ $labels.instance }}"
```

#### 6.5.7.2 ELK Stack Integration Example

**Step 1: Configure Rsyslog to Forward to Logstash**

```bash
# /etc/rsyslog.d/dnsmasq-logstash.conf

#### Forward all dnsmasq logs to Logstash
:programname, startswith, "dnsmasq" @@logstash.company.com:5140

#### Continue logging locally
& ~
```

**Step 2: Logstash Configuration**

```ruby
# /etc/logstash/conf.d/dnsmasq.conf

input {
  syslog {
    port => 5140
    type => "dnsmasq"
  }
}

filter {
  if [type] == "dnsmasq" {
    grok {
      match => {
        "message" => [
          # DNS query pattern
          "query\[%{WORD:query_type}\] %{HOSTNAME:query_name} from %{IP:client_ip}",
          
          # DNS reply pattern
          "reply %{HOSTNAME:reply_name} is %{IP:reply_ip}",
          
          # DHCP pattern
          "DHCP%{WORD:dhcp_message}\(%{WORD:interface}\) %{IP:dhcp_ip} %{MAC:dhcp_mac}( %{HOSTNAME:dhcp_hostname})?",
          
          # Cache statistics pattern
          "cache size %{NUMBER:cache_size:int}, %{NUMBER:cache_insertions:int}/%{NUMBER:cache_evictions:int}",
          
          # Upstream server pattern
          "server %{IP:upstream_ip}#%{NUMBER:upstream_port}: queries sent %{NUMBER:queries_sent:int}, retried %{NUMBER:retries:int}, failed %{NUMBER:failures:int}.*avg\. latency %{NUMBER:avg_latency:float}ms"
        ]
      }
    }
    
    # Add GeoIP for client locations (optional)
    if [client_ip] {
      geoip {
        source => "client_ip"
      }
    }
  }
}

output {
  if [type] == "dnsmasq" {
    elasticsearch {
      hosts => ["elasticsearch.company.com:9200"]
      index => "dnsmasq-%{+YYYY.MM.dd}"
    }
  }
}
```

**Step 3: Kibana Visualizations**

- **Query Volume by Type**: Bar chart of A, AAAA, PTR, CNAME query counts
- **Top Queried Domains**: Table of most frequently queried domain names
- **DHCP Assignment Map**: Geo map of DHCP client locations (if GeoIP enabled)
- **Error Log Timeline**: Timeline of error messages with severity highlighting

## 6.6 Testing Strategy

### 6.6.1 Testing Philosophy and Rationale

Dnsmasq employs a **pragmatic testing approach** that reflects its maturity as a stable, widely-deployed C codebase serving millions of installations across embedded systems, routers, and enterprise networks. Unlike modern software projects that prioritize unit test coverage, dnsmasq's testing strategy emphasizes integration testing, real-world validation, and conservative code change practices.

#### 6.6.1.1 Architectural Testing Approach

The testing strategy aligns with the system's monolithic, single-process architecture documented in Technical Specification Section 6.1. Since all functionality executes within a single address space (`/usr/sbin/dnsmasq`) with direct function calls and shared memory structures, traditional unit testing with mocking frameworks provides limited value. Instead, end-to-end integration testing validates the complete service stack—DNS resolution, DHCP lease management, network protocol handling—as they interact in production deployments.

**Core Testing Principles**:

| Principle | Implementation | Rationale |
|-----------|---------------|-----------|
| **Integration Over Isolation** | Autopkgtest validates complete service workflows | Tests real-world service interactions rather than isolated functions |
| **Field Validation** | Millions of installations across distributions | Diverse deployment scenarios exercise edge cases organically |
| **Conservative Changes** | Minimal code churn, careful review process | Reduces testing burden through stability-first development |
| **Compiler-Driven Quality** | `-Wall -W` flags treat warnings as defects | Catches common C programming errors at compile time |

#### 6.6.1.2 Testing Maturity Model

Dnsmasq operates in a **maintenance and stability phase** rather than rapid feature development, influencing testing priorities:

**Development Phase Characteristics**:
- **Codebase Age**: 20+ years in production
- **Release Cadence**: Conservative, stability-focused releases
- **Feature Scope**: Well-defined, stable feature set
- **Deployment Scale**: Validated across millions of installations
- **Platform Diversity**: Linux, BSD, macOS, Android, OpenWrt

This maturity enables reliance on extensive field testing that would be impractical for early-stage projects. The vast deployment base provides comprehensive validation across hardware platforms, network configurations, and edge cases that automated test suites struggle to replicate.

#### 6.6.1.3 What Is Not Tested (Intentional Gaps)

The following testing practices are **intentionally absent**, representing deliberate architectural decisions rather than oversights:

**No Traditional Unit Testing Framework**:
- **Evidence**: No `tests/` directory, no CUnit/Check/Google Test dependencies, no test targets in Makefile
- **Rationale**: Monolithic architecture with tight component coupling makes unit testing isolation impractical without extensive mocking infrastructure
- **Mitigation**: Integration tests validate component interactions as they occur in production

**No Continuous Integration Infrastructure**:
- **Evidence**: No GitHub Actions workflows, no GitLab CI configuration, no Jenkins pipelines
- **Rationale**: Traditional C project with manual review process by core maintainers
- **Mitigation**: Distribution maintainers run autopkgtest during package validation, providing CI-like validation at package level

**No Automated Security Testing**:
- **Evidence**: No fuzzing integration (AFL, libFuzzer), no automated DNSSEC validation tests
- **Rationale**: Security validation occurs through manual code review and external security audits
- **Mitigation**: DNSSEC implementation validated through operational deployment, fuzzing performed manually by maintainers

### 6.6.2 Testing Approach

#### 6.6.2.1 Integration Testing (Primary Test Strategy)

##### 6.6.2.1.1 Autopkgtest Framework

**Location**: `submodules/dnsmasq-debian/debian/tests/`

Autopkgtest serves as the primary automated testing infrastructure, providing comprehensive integration validation for Debian and Ubuntu package releases. This framework validates the complete system stack—service startup, network configuration, protocol handling, and graceful shutdown—in isolated container environments.

**Test Control Definition** (`debian/tests/control`):

Six distinct test suites validate different configuration scenarios and feature combinations:

| Test Suite | Purpose | Key Dependencies | Restrictions |
|------------|---------|-----------------|--------------|
| **compile-time-options** | Validates enabled compile-time features | dnsmasq, dnsmasq-base | needs-root, isolation-container |
| **compile-time-options+lua** | Validates Lua scripting integration | dnsmasq, dnsmasq-base-lua | needs-root, isolation-container |
| **get-address+query-dns+check-utils** | Comprehensive DHCP, DNS, utility testing | bind9, dnsmasq, dnsmasq-utils, ifupdown | needs-root, allow-stderr, isolation-container |
| **get-address+query-dns+lua+alt** | Lua scripting with alternative configuration | bind9, dnsmasq-base-lua, ifupdown | needs-root, allow-stderr, isolation-container |
| **get-address+query-dns+sysv+alt** | SysV init script compatibility testing | bind9, dnsmasq-base, ifupdown | needs-root, allow-stderr, isolation-container |
| **verify-fix-to-bug-871958** | Regression test for postfix interaction | dnsmasq, postfix, resolvconf | needs-root, isolation-container |

**Test Environment Requirements**:
- **Root Privileges**: Required for network interface creation, service management, port binding (53, 67, 69)
- **Container Isolation**: Prevents test side effects on host system, enables parallel test execution
- **Network Namespace Support**: Creates virtual network interfaces and isolated network stacks

##### 6.6.2.1.2 Test Execution Workflow

```mermaid
graph TB
    Start[Test Starts] --> Cleanup[Stop Conflicting Services]
    Cleanup --> PurgeResolved[possibly_purge_resolved<br/>Free port 53]
    PurgeResolved --> StopServices[stop_dnsmasq_bind_networking<br/>Clean state]
    StopServices --> ConfigNet[configure_and_start_networking<br/>Create veth pairs, netns]
    ConfigNet --> ConfigBind[configure_and_start_bind<br/>Authoritative DNS zone]
    ConfigBind --> ConfigDnsmasq[configure_and_start_dnsmasq<br/>Forwarder + DHCP server]
    ConfigDnsmasq --> StartNet[Start networking.service]
    StartNet --> StartBind[Start named.service]
    StartBind --> StartDnsmasq[Start dnsmasq.service]
    StartDnsmasq --> WaitReady[Wait for service ready]
    
    WaitReady --> TestDHCP[get_address_on_veth1_and_check_the_result<br/>DHCP lease acquisition]
    TestDHCP --> TestDNS[query_test_zone_records_and_check_the_result<br/>DNS resolution validation]
    TestDNS --> TestUtils{Utils test?}
    TestUtils -->|Yes| TestUtilsExec[check_utils<br/>dhcp_lease_time, dhcp_release]
    TestUtils -->|No| LuaTest
    TestUtilsExec --> LuaTest{Lua mode?}
    
    LuaTest -->|Yes| CheckLuaLog[check_lua_log<br/>Verify script execution]
    LuaTest -->|No| Validate
    CheckLuaLog --> Validate[Pattern Matching Validation]
    
    Validate --> Result{All patterns match?}
    Result -->|Yes| Success[Exit 0 - PASS]
    Result -->|No| Failure[match_or_exit fails<br/>Exit non-zero - FAIL]
    
    style Start fill:#e1f5ff
    style Success fill:#d4edda
    style Failure fill:#f8d7da
    style Validate fill:#fff4e1
```

**Test Orchestration Functions** (`debian/tests/functions`):

| Function | Responsibility | Key Actions |
|----------|---------------|-------------|
| `possibly_purge_resolved()` | Port 53 conflict resolution | Removes systemd-resolved if present, frees DNS port |
| `stop_dnsmasq_bind_networking()` | Service cleanup | Stops dnsmasq, bind9, networking services for clean state |
| `configure_and_start_networking()` | Virtual network setup | Creates dummy0, veth0/veth1 pair, clientnet namespace |
| `configure_and_start_bind()` | Upstream DNS configuration | Configures BIND authoritative zone for autopkg.test domain |
| `configure_and_start_dnsmasq()` | Dnsmasq service setup | Configures listening addresses, DHCP ranges, forwarding rules |
| `check_compile_time_options()` | Feature validation | Verifies expected compile-time features enabled |
| `get_address_on_veth1_and_check_the_result()` | DHCP functionality test | Acquires lease via dhcpcd, validates IP assignment |
| `query_test_zone_records_and_check_the_result()` | DNS functionality test | Performs dig queries, validates responses |
| `check_utils()` | Utility validation | Tests dhcp_lease_time and dhcp_release utilities |
| `check_lua_log()` | Lua integration test | Verifies Lua script executed on DHCP events |
| `match_or_exit()` | Assertion mechanism | Pattern-matches output, exits with failure on mismatch |

##### 6.6.2.1.3 Test Environment Architecture

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "Test Container Environment"
        subgraph "Root Network Namespace"
            Bind[BIND DNS Server<br/>192.168.141.1:53<br/>Authoritative for autopkg.test]
            Dnsmasq[Dnsmasq Service<br/>192.168.142.1:53<br/>Forwarder + DHCP]

        end
        
        Dnsmasq -->|DNS Queries| Bind
        Dnsmasq -.->|DHCP OFFER| Veth1
        Veth1 -.->|DHCP DISCOVER/REQUEST| Dnsmasq
        Veth1 -.->|DNS Queries| Dnsmasq
        DHCPClient --> Veth1
        DigClient --> Veth1
    end
    
    subgraph "Test Fixtures"
        ZoneFile[db.autopkg.test<br/>SOA, NS, A records]
        DnsmasqConf[dnsmasq-autopkgtest.conf<br/>Isolated configuration]

        Patterns[*.patterns files<br/>Expected output]
    end
    
    Bind --> ZoneFile
    Dnsmasq --> DnsmasqConf
